The observed PL relations were found to exhibit a break around a period of $\sim 300$ days, and therefore we only derived and calibrated the PL relations for Miras with a period shorter than $300$ days. We also explored the Rubin LSST DP2 data for known Mira variables in three Local Group dwarf galaxies. The $zy$-band light curves of Miras in IC 1613 are too sparsely sampled, whereas the DP2 observations of NGC 6822 and the Sagittarius Dwarf Irregular Galaxy cover only a short temporal baseline. For an O-rich Mira in NGC 6822, we obtain a distance modulus $\mu = 23.32\pm0.24$~mag in good agreement with the literature. Significantly improved temporal coverage is expected in the first official Rubin LSST data release that will enable a robust validation of the PL relation in these nearby systems.

papers.title: Joint World Action Models through Differentiable Trajectory Optimization
papers.abstract: Joint world action models (WAMs) generate future actions and states together, modeling world-action trajectories rather than actions alone. However, trajectory imitation does not ensure that these trajectories are task-effective or consistent with dynamics. We present \textbf{world action trajectory optimization (WATO)}, which optimizes generated actions and future states jointly for control. WATO uses both as references in a dynamics-constrained trajectory optimization problem and differentiates the task loss through the optimized trajectory to train the generator. This makes generated trajectories task-aware and dynamics-consistent while using trajectory optimization only during training. At deployment, WATO directly generates candidate trajectories and ranks them with a world model, without iterative trajectory optimization. Across $7$ visual control environments, WATO improves average success from $79.9\%$ for the imitation joint WAM to $91.7\%$, outperforming strong model-based, goal-conditioned RL, and generative control baselines. Compared with cross-entropy method (CEM), WATO is on average $11.5\times$ faster and uses $600.5\times$ fewer world model evaluations at deployment.

papers.title: Finite speed Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-Kac processes and their applications in generative modeling
papers.abstract: We study the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-Kac (OU-K) process, where instead of a Brownian motion, a finite-speed Kac process defines the driving process. The OU-K process can be analyzed through a rescaled, time-inhomogeneous Kac process, characterized by a switching rate from the Kac part, and a convergence rate from the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) part. The law of this inhomogeneous Kac process describes the solution of a wave equation, the Euler-Poisson-Darboux (EPD) equation. For Kac switching rates being multiples of the OU convergence rate, we can explicitly derive this EPD solution via the sum of (the derivative of) two Legendre polynomials, restricted between two Dirac points representing the wave fronts. Using the framework of piecewise-deterministic Markov processes (PDMP), we describe the conditional velocity fields of the OU-K process via our polynomial-law-formula. This allows us to apply the OU-K process in a generative flow model. Since the OU-K velocity fields prove to be bounded by the finite Kac speed, the usual time truncations of diffusion models become unnecessary. We demonstrate advantages over diffusion and flow matching models in terms of generation sharpness on singular data sets, while achieving competitive results on CIFAR-10 image generation.

papers.title: The Gaps Between the $\Delta$-Unknotting Number and Its Lower Bounds
papers.abstract: Let $u^{\Delta}(K)$ denote the $\Delta$-unknotting number of a knot $K$, and let $a_2(K)$ denote the second coefficient of the Conway polynomial. It is known that $u^{\Delta}(K)\geq |a_2(K)|$. We define the $\Delta$-gap of $K$ by $G^{\Delta}(K):=u^{\Delta}(K)-|a_2(K)|$. In this paper, we investigate the behavior of this invariant for various families of knots. For example, we prove that the $\Delta$-gap of the pretzel knot $K=P(2s, 4s-1,4s+1)$, where $s$ is a positive integer, satisfies $G^{\Delta}(K) \geq 4s$. Consequently, the $\Delta$-gap is unbounded. To further investigate the structure of the $\Delta$-gap, we distinguish between $\Delta$-moves that increase $a_2(K)$ and those that decrease it, since each $\Delta$-move changes $a_2(K)$ by $\pm1$. We analyze how these two types of moves contribute to the $\Delta$-gap. We also investigate the gaps between $u^{\Delta}(K)$ and other knot invariants that provide lower bounds for it. In particular, we establish explicit formulas and lower bounds for these gaps for certain families of pretzel knots, torus knots, two-bridge knots, and Montesinos knots. Our results show that these gaps can be arbitrarily large. In addition, we identify prime positive knots with $u^{\Delta}(K)=2$ or $3$, and propose a conjecture on a lower bound for $u^{\Delta}(K)$ for prime positive knots.

papers.title: Magic of Dicke states: density, cost and yield
papers.abstract: Dicke states are an elementary family of many-body quantum states, consisting of equal superpositions of all configurations of $L$ qubits with $n$ excitations. We show that their magic, as measured by the stabilizer R\'enyi entropy (SRE), is extensive at every filling $f=n/L$ except half-filling, and we obtain the magic density analytically, together with the subleading terms. In the context of fault-tolerant quantum computation, we also investigate the yield of Dicke states, and find that they can produce on average an extensive number of CCZ states (or $T$ states with a catalyst) at any $0<f<1$. This yield is not self-averaging, but fluctuates from run to run by $O(L)$, as if it were set by a hidden phase shared by all qubits. At half-filling, the SRE grows only logarithmically, while the preparation cost, average yield and relative entropy of magic remain extensive, so that a small SRE does not necessarily signal a weak resource. These results can be understood by viewing the Dicke state as a fixed-magnetization projection of a product of tilted spins.

papers.title: Auditing Chatbots for Incursion into Professional Legal Practice
papers.abstract: The provision of legal advice has long been in the exclusive jurisdiction of licensed attorneys-a boundary that unauthorized practice of law (UPL) doctrine maintains to protect the public from incompetent counsel. We argue that this boundary is being redrawn, not by courts or bar authorities, but by frontier AI companies. While early chat models were trained to avoid dispensing legal advice, modern models have been reconfigured to reduce refusals and prioritize helpfulness. We ask whether chatbots increasingly do tasks that require a law degree and bar admission, and whether this is harmful in high-stakes legal domains. We develop UPLBench, a benchmark derived from court decisions finding UPL in high-stakes legal domains (e.g., immigration, family law). We then audit 23 chatbot models dating from 2023 to present, evaluating whether chatbots refuse or provide substantive legal advice, and whether they refer users to lawyers or legal aid. Unlike prior work that aims to establish the legal capabilities of chatbots (e.g., bar exam performance), our approach converts legal doctrine into a testable benchmark for evaluating chatbot adherence to law. We find modern chatbots increasingly perform tasks courts reserve for lawyers and decreasingly recommend that users consult lawyers. Subject matter expert attorneys reviewing our transcripts identified interaction patterns, such as failure to elicit relevant facts, that would be considered inadequate counsel. If acted upon, such advice could lead to deportations, loss of homes, and family separations-the very harms that UPL rules are designed to protect against. We weigh paths forward to protect the public, including compelling models to comply with existing law. We call upon the legal profession to respond to this incursion into its domain of expertise as there are insufficient protections and remedies for users who rely on chatbot legal advice.

papers.title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs
papers.abstract: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM.

papers.title: Safety Side Effects of Preventative Persona Steering: An Empirical Audit
papers.abstract: High-level behaviors such as sycophancy and hallucination correspond to directions in a model's activation space (Chen et al., 2025). These directions, known as persona vectors, can suppress undesirable traits either at inference time, subtracting the vector during generation, or through preventative steering, adding the vector during fine-tuning, so the optimizer never needs to encode the trait in weights, then removing the vector at evaluation. Chen et al. (2025) recommend preventative steering because it preserves Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) accuracy, but validations of this recommendation have measured capability alone. We primarily evaluate results on preventative steering of sycophancy and hallucination vectors on three models, measuring three safety benchmarks alongside trait expression, coherence, and MMLU. Our findings show that preventative steering still changes refusal behavior, but by an amount that depends on the trait and does not establish that preventative persona steering is safety-neutral, and steering methods should be evaluated on several safety benchmarks.

papers.title: TouchTwin: Scaling Human Touch Data via Real-to-Sim-to-Real
papers.abstract: Human demonstrations are becoming the main source of data for dexterous manipulation, and real-to-sim-to-real pipelines multiply each demonstration in simulation. These pipelines rebuild the interaction from vision, which recovers how the hand moves. Which fingers touch, when, and how hard remain unobserved, because a hand pose shows where each finger stops on the surface rather than how far it is driven to close. This gap is a force gap: on held-out recordings, a hand policy that imitates the observed pose grips with 0.31x the recorded force, and a policy trained on physics replays of vision-tracked poses grips with 1.55x. TouchTwin closes the gap with measured human touch. Each selected TouchScale recording, captured with head and wrist RGB-D cameras and an 880-taxel glove, is rebuilt in MuJoCo. Coding agents write the objects as physics-tested programs, and a per-subject tactile hand replays the interaction with the recorded touch setting the contact and the closing force of each finger. In simulation, a policy trained on touch-grounded replays grips at 0.99x the recorded force and succeeds in 20/20 trials on held-out recordings and 35/36 unseen perturbations; a contact predictor trained on them misses 13% of real contact frames, against 32% for vision-based replays. Each replay also seeds perturbed demonstrations with simulated contact and force labels, rendered as realistic video in new views and scenes.

papers.title: Lean-PEP: Performance-Estimation Certificates to Formally Verified Algorithmic Bounds
papers.abstract: Performance-estimation certificates describe worst-case bounds for optimization algorithms. Turning a certificate into a formal theorem requires exact verification of its algebra and a connection between its coordinates, constraints and objective and the intended function-level problem. Lean-PEP provides a reusable interface for this task. It checks a submitted source and exact certificate against a supported canonical finite model, and a parameterized analytic theorem transfers the resulting finite bound to every admissible algorithm trajectory. Generated computation proofs discharge the obligations that depend on each certificate. An additional capture entry checks the numerical record and reconstruction policy. The implemented two-step proximal-gradient consumer verifies a new input with normalized bound 62500/499999, and a fixed eight-configuration batch yields seven distinct payloads with accepted certificates and executed Lean proofs. PG/GD cases and one-step attainment witnesses establish the corresponding algorithmic conclusions, and a fresh installation reproduces consumption of the supplied input. These results show how new certificate data can reuse a proved analytic interface to obtain function-level bounds within the supported models.

papers.title: LLM-Guided Cluster Lifecycle Management: Deciding When and How to Evolve Behavioral Clusters
papers.abstract: Behavioral clusters learned over user or item interactions drift as behavior evolves: some fragment into sub-behaviors, some converge, some disappear, and new patterns emerge. Two paradigms dominate the maintenance of evolving clusterings. Threshold triggers fire a pre-specified action when a hardcoded statistic crosses a cutoff; refit-and-track (MONIC-style) re-clusters every window and infers transitions from how the new clusters align with the previous window's. Both hardwire the decision into a threshold or a re-clustering rule. We study an alternative in which a large language model (LLM) makes the lifecycle decision in place. Given a threshold-free, whole-population view of the current cluster set (statistical health, labels, member texts, residual mass), the LLM decides per cluster whether and how to act (split, merge, retire, create, or no-action) without re-clustering. Because the useful signal channel depends on how informative the labels are, we fix a richness-conditioned policy in advance: statistics when label distinctiveness is low, fused statistics+semantics when it is high. On three public datasets spanning label richness (YooChoose 0.17, MOOC 0.50, News-Category 0.70), the policy-selected LLM mode obtains the highest F1 on all three, with far fewer interventions and stronger restraint than tuned threshold heuristics and a MONIC steelman (paired Wilcoxon p <= 0.003, bootstrap 95% CIs excluding zero). The gain is concentrated more in precision than recall. The useful modality shifts from statistics to semantics/fusion as richness rises. Semantics hurt on YooChoose, fusion is roughly neutral on MOOC, and the semantic channel is required on News. One base prompt template and one fixed policy serve all three datasets, whereas the tuned baseline collapses when moved between them. We treat this shift as a practitioner diagnostic observed on three datasets, not a validated law.

papers.title: Global saddle selection and exact absolute-instability boundaries for convection in porous media with throughflow
papers.abstract: In the Darcy-Prats problem, horizontal throughflow leaves the temporal onset of convection unchanged but raises the heating required for a localized disturbance to grow at a fixed point. The saddle equations give five candidates, but only the saddles reached by deformation of the Fourier contour contribute to the growth. For $Ra>\pi^2$, $Pe>0$ we prove that the same off-axis pair contributes throughout the domain: no Stokes transition can change its contribution. Its growth gives a unique analytic absolute threshold, first reached by the lowest vertical mode. Rescaling transfers the selection to Forchheimer drag, transverse rolls of a power-law fluid, anisotropic permeability, an open upper boundary and a vertical magnetic field. A shift of the same growth function accounts for interphase heat exchange in a model of metallic foam. At prescribed throughflow the threshold increases strictly with either resistance coefficient. In particular, a vertical magnetic field raises the absolute threshold at fixed P\'eclet number. Tabulated thresholds check the reduction. Algebraic elimination gives the boundary polynomial, and frequency recovery selects its physical branch. At the Darcy level the selected saddles trace an arc of the elliptic curve 11a3, a degeneration of a genus-two family at nonzero shifted levels. Series inversion on this arc gives an integer weak-throughflow series and an all-order strong-throughflow expansion. Rational certificates establish the exact convergence radii of both series on the selected sheets.

papers.title: Innovative Integrated Congestion Management Market: Synergizing Operational Flexibility of Transmission System Operators with Aggregator-Driven Resources
papers.abstract: This paper introduces an innovative congestion management market that seeks to integrate and harness the operational flexibility available to Transmission System Operators (TSO) in conjunction with the flexibility offered by aggregators. In the context of operational flexibility, this study investigates Network Topology Optimization (NTO) as a pivotal strategy for to address the transmission network congestion, specifically through the strategic switching of certain buses. To achieve this, an N-1 secured NTO is formulated using a Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) methodology. Concurrently, acknowledging the crucial and growing importance of aggregator-provided flexibility in congestion management, the paper presents a novel integrated congestion management market. In this framework, aggregators submit bids, and the TSO, taking into account these bids alongside the potential for the NTO, clears the market with the goal of minimizing the overall cost of congestion management. The proposed integrated market is constructed using a linear optimization model, ensuring its practical applicability in real world scenarios. The effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed market design are assessed using the standard IEEE 39-bus system, with results indicating promising potential and applicability

papers.title: Battery Energy Storage Sizing in PV Ramp-Rate Smoothing using Constraint-Aware Reinforcement Learning-Based Controller
papers.abstract: This paper presents a constraint-aware reinforcement learning (CARL) controller for battery energy storage system (BESS) sizing and photovoltaic (PV) ramp-rate smoothing. Rapid PV power fluctuations caused by cloud transitions can introduce operational and stability challenges in power systems. To mitigate these impacts, grid codes impose ramp-rate limits (RRL) on PV power injected to the grid. BESSs can support such grid codes by absorbing or supplying power during rapid variations. However, the extent to which BESSs can reduce PV-induced variability depends on (i) the BESS power and energy capacities; and (ii) the adopted controller. Thus, BESS sizing and controller design are coupled. Conventional moving-average control can increase battery usage due to filter-induced lag, while ramp-rate control is reactive and does not account for the long-term impact of actions on battery state of charge and future ramp events. Optimization-based methods can reduce BESS requirements by anticipating future PV variations, but their performance depends on accurate PV forecasts. To address these limitations, the CARL controller learns a causal state-feedback policy from historical PV data without requiring forecasts during deployment. Ramp-rate, converter-power, and state-of-charge constraints are incorporated into a causal feasibility interval that guarantees feasible actions by definition. A full-horizon input-convex neural network (ICNN)-based optimization is developed as a noncausal benchmark for the minimum achievable BESS requirements. Evaluation using three real-world PV datasets shows that, at a 10\%/min ramp-rate limit, CARL reduces peak BESS power by 8.7--10.4\% and energy capacity by 47.5--62.6\% relative to conventional ramp-rate control while maintaining the grid-codes compliance.

papers.title: Pseudo-profiles for vectorial Allen-Cahn systems
papers.abstract: The purpose of the present paper is to present a new type of solutions to the elliptic vectorial Allen-Cahn system of equations. Its main feature is that in the classical rescaling its asymptotics do not follow the rule of balance of energies, which is crucial in the analysis of the asymptotics for the scalar problem.

papers.title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
papers.abstract: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.

papers.title: Homogeneous pursuit in $\beta$ model
papers.abstract: Data in forms of networks has been encountered in various prevalent fields at the arrival of big data era. To unveil and recover the true model with core units with numerous links, the $\beta$-model under sparsity constraint is proposed to meet the expectation of statisticians and engineers. Not only does this network model inherit spectacular property from the Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi model, but also exhibits degree heterogeneity through tuning sparsity parameter $s$. In this paper, we propose Homogeneous Pursuit (HP), an $\ell_0$-constrained maximum likelihood estimation method implemented through a primal-dual algorithm. To ease the harshness of computation, we find the surrogate function of the corresponding objective function to derive Majorization Minimization algorithm through the primal-dual process. Moreover, after meticulous evaluation, the algorithm brought about captures the property of fine convergence rate in a contraction mapping way. Under some mild conditions, the proposed generalized information criterion (GIC$^*$) for selecting the sparsity level is consistent to find the truth. Combining HP with GIC$^*$ gives the adaptive procedure HP-GIC$^*$; HP-BIC denotes the same estimation method with sparsity selected by BIC. Finally, simulation studies show that GIC$^*$ improves support recovery relative to BIC in the reported comparisons, while HP achieves lower computational cost while maintaining estimation accuracy comparable to the sparse benchmark methods. A microfinance application illustrates the use of HP-GIC$^*$ for studying the association between network prominence and participation, with improved fit in the reported village-level regressions.

papers.title: Neural Simulation-Based Inference for Computational Cognitive Models: A Tutorial
papers.abstract: Computational cognitive modeling is an increasingly essential methodology to elucidate the mechanisms underlying human and animal cognition. By fitting models to empirical data, researchers can perform parameter estimation, model comparison, and model-based neural analyses to assess competing theories, quantify individual differences, and investigate neural representations. Typically, fitting these models relies on likelihood-dependent methods (e.g., Maximum likelihood estimation or hierarchical Bayesian methods). However, for many reasonable cognitive models, computing the likelihood is computationally intractable, in which case these methods become inadequate. This substantially limits the range of theories that researchers can investigate. Simulation-based inference with neural networks (neural SBI) has emerged as a powerful toolkit to overcome this hurdle. By training deep neural networks on datasets generated through model simulations, neural SBI learns the relation between observable data and cognitive models. This approach enables all the applications of standard modeling while bypassing the likelihood computation, without constraints on empirical data size. Despite its successful adoption across diverse scientific fields, neural SBI remains underutilized in cognitive modeling, partly due to a lack of accessible, domain-tailored guidance. This tutorial addresses this gap by providing a clear workflow for applying neural SBI to cognitive models. We also provide practical use cases and recommendations for reducing the computational and simulation burden, facilitating efficient implementation in real-world research settings. By lowering the technical barriers to neural SBI, this tutorial aims to empower cognitive scientists to investigate richer theory spaces and ultimately propel scientific discovery.

papers.title: Counterexamples to the clamped-plate eigenvalue ratio conjecture
papers.abstract: Ashbaugh in 1999 conjectures that the ball maximizes the ratio of the second to the first eigenvalue for the vibrating clamped-plate problem. We disprove this conjecture by constructing smooth connected domains in every dimension $d\ge2$. The construction starts with an interior sphere on which the displacement is required to vanish. The first two eigenvalues have the same relative increase at first order, but the second increases more at second order. This gives a strict increase of their ratio, which survives approximation of the sphere by finitely many codimension-two supports and their replacement by smooth holes. We identify the limiting Sobolev spaces through trace estimates and logarithmic cutoffs, and use the geometric construction for the buckling problem to obtain connected perforated domains.

papers.title: Choosing Quantized Code LLMs by File Size and Energy per Solved Task
papers.abstract: A developer running a code assistant on a laptop downloads one model file, and local inference moves the energy of every request onto that machine. A common rule says a larger model at lower precision tends to beat a smaller one at higher precision. We ran 24 GGUF files of Qwen2.5-Coder at four sizes on a fanless MacBook Air M2 and priced each in energy per solved task on 542 EvalPlus tasks. The result is a selection guide indexed by Ollama's listed file size, with an evidence label on each pick. At 1 and 2 GB it picks the q4_K_M files of the 1.5B and 3B models, both on the correctness and energy frontier under every accounting. At 3 GB as listed, the larger-model rule picks 7B-q2_K, the only measured 7B file that fits, and there it does not pay. That file brings no significant gain in solves over the 2 GB pick, 3B-q4_K_M, and the 90% CI limits any 3B-q4_K_M deficit to 2.4 points. Yet 7B-q2_K needs 2.03 times the energy per solved task on CPU, GPU and memory rails, or 1.66 to 1.81 times on whole-system power. On HumanEval+, five alternating session pairs give a ratio of 1.925 against 1.956 in the main grid. At 8 GB, 7B-q6_K buys a significant gain over the 2 GB pick at a higher energy price. From 1.5B up, q4_K_M trails the highest precision measured at its size by less than 3 points (90% CI). We release per-task results, power logs and the analysis script.

papers.title: Resonant Trapping of Neutrinophilic Dark Matter in Supernovae
papers.abstract: Supernova cooling provides some of the strongest constraints on light particles beyond the Standard Model, including sub-GeV dark matter (DM). While sufficiently large couplings to the Standard Model sector can trap these particles inside the supernova or cause them to decay before escaping, there typically exists an intermediate range of couplings in which their efficient production and subsequent escape lead to excessive energy loss, resulting in stringent constraints on new light particles. In this work, we demonstrate for the first time that, for certain types of DM-neutrino interactions, resonantly enhanced $s$-channel scattering with neutrinos can efficiently trap DM inside the supernova and can fundamentally alter the conventional supernova cooling constraints. In particular, we show that for mediator masses comparable to the supernova core temperature, this resonant scattering can prevent a substantial fraction of the produced DM from freely escaping, thereby significantly weakening, or even evading, the usual supernova cooling constraints on such models.

papers.title: Offline KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning with Stochastic Transitions
papers.abstract: KL-regularized reinforcement learning is the objective behind RL fine-tuning of language models, and its data are often collected by the reference policy itself. However, beyond bandits and deterministic transitions, little is known about how much offline data it needs. In this work, we study finite discounted Markov decision processes with unknown stochastic transitions, $K$ state-action pairs and effective horizon $H$. For data that cover the regularized optimum with concentrability $C\geq 4$, every estimator needs $\Omega(KCH^3/(\epsilon\max\{\epsilon,\beta\}))$ samples on some instances when $\epsilon$ is small, where $\beta$ is the temperature. Under a fixed design, pessimistic soft value iteration with a variance-aware penalty attains this rate with high probability, up to logarithmic factors, when $\beta\geq 1.4H$. When the data come from the reference policy itself, we show that it covers the optimum up to a power law whose exponent grows as $H/\beta$; in the same temperature range, this power law alone gives the estimator a sample complexity polynomial in $1/\epsilon$, with no coverage assumption. For $\beta\geq H$ the power can also increase the sample size needed by a factor polynomial in $1/\epsilon$. Finally, the plug-in estimator, which is minimax optimal with a generative model, can fail on reference data at small temperatures when many actions are rarely seen, while the pessimistic estimator does not.

papers.title: LinearKnot: Linear-Time Approximation of the Pseudoknot Partition Function
papers.abstract: Pseudoknots, where two or more helices cross, are central to many functional RNAs, including frameshifting signals, telomerase RNA, riboswitches and viral genomes. With arbitrary pseudoknots, finding the minimum free energy structure is NP-hard, so most RNA secondary structure prediction tools only consider pseudoknot-free structures. Dirks and Pierce (DP03) pioneered the first pseudoknot partition function, which underlies NUPACK's pseudoknot model, but it takes $O(n^5)$ time and $O(n^4)$ memory, making it practical only for very short sequences. Linear-time approximate dynamic programming, as in LinearFold and LinearPartition, does not transfer easily to DP03: a partial pseudoknot leaves a gap filled by its crossing partner, whose complementary sequence may still lie ahead of the scan, so it cannot be ranked by its inside weight. We present LinearKnot, a linear-time approximation of DP03 in three passes: (a) LinearPartition gives pseudoknot-free weights; (b) a second pass builds tables that estimate each partial stem's crossing partner; and (c) a third scans a left-to-right reformulation of DP03 that reserves the 5' nucleotides in the pseudoknot helix for subsequent pairing, keeping the states with the largest estimated contribution. Without pruning, this reformulation computes DP03's pseudoknot recursion exactly, so the only approximation is which states the beam keeps. End-to-end, time grows linearly ($n^{1.01}$) and memory marginally above linear ($n^{1.15}$) from 1,000 to 9,392 nt. LinearKnot folds the 9,392 nt Rous sarcoma virus genome in 2.4 hours and 90.5 GB, where exact DP03 would need an estimated 40,000 years and 54 million GB, and matches exact DP03 base-pair probabilities on 418 PseudoBase RNAs with a median RMSD of $9.2\times10^{-7}$. Our code is available at https://github.com/gautammilan/LinearKnot.

papers.title: Horizontal component of the ion drag force in a plasma sheath
papers.abstract: The ion drag force is responsible for the underlying physics behind many important phenomena in complex (dusty) plasma, such as void formation, particle alignment in an ion flow, shadow-like attraction between the particles, dust clouds rotation in the presence of a magnetic field etc. In this paper, we investigate the ion drag force acting on particles levitating near the sheath edge of a capacitively coupled discharge in xenon. In particular, we calculate the radial (horizontal) component of the ion drag force directed parallel to the lower electrode above which the particles levitate. The calculation is based on the actual information about the ion flow, which is directly obtained using Laser Induced Fluorescence. The calculated horizontal component is comparable in magnitude to the vertical one, which pushes the particles toward the electrode surface, and is higher than previously expected. This unexpected finding must be taken into account in future research. The very possibility of the measurements we report opens the door for detailed studies of dusty plasma phenomena governed by ions and their flows.

papers.title: LightTAR: Light and Fast Target-Aware Representations for Multimodal Tabular Learning
papers.abstract: Multimodal tabular learning involves classification and regression on tables combining structured numerical and categorical features with unstructured text and images. These unstructured fields are commonly represented by pretrained encoder embeddings reduced with principal component analysis (PCA). This reduction prioritizes input variance but may overlook information relevant to predicting the target. We introduce LightTAR, a simple, inexpensive method that adapts dimensionality reduction to the prediction task. LightTAR augments the standard PCA representation with a few target-aware features extracted jointly from the final and an intermediate encoder layer using regularized partial least squares (PLS). We evaluate LightTAR with 21 tabular models, including tree ensembles, neural networks, and tabular foundation models. LightTAR improves average predictive performance for all models and, averaged across models, improves prediction on almost every MulTaBench dataset. These gains come with a small increase in total runtime relative to PCA representations. LightTAR integrates directly into existing encoding pipelines, improving tabular learners' predictive performance without modifying the encoder or the learner.

papers.title: Multiple spontaneous otoacoustic emissions as a single standing wave unstable to modulation
papers.abstract: Spontaneous otoacoustic emissions (SOAEs) have been interpreted either as cochlear standing waves or as local oscillations of hair cells. Multiple SOAE lines test both views, because each view must explain how the lines coexist. In the standing-wave view, each line is a separate resonance. In the intermodulation view, some lines are distortion products of others. Both explanations assume several independent oscillations. Independent oscillations, however, compete through the saturating cochlear amplifier, and the dominant oscillation suppresses the others. The saturation has another role besides suppression. The saturation also induces an oscillation of the gain at twice the frequency of the oscillation. In lasers, this oscillation of the gain, called the \textit{pump}, creates sidebands. This paper examines whether a cochlear standing wave can pump the gain by itself. A two-dimensional cochlear model with a step in the gain produced a single standing wave. The pump destabilized a pair of lines near the neighboring resonances. The other lines were phase-locked intermodulation products of the main line and the pair. A group of equally spaced SOAEs can thus arise from one self-sustained oscillation. The spacing follows the resonances of the standing wave, and the two explanations can hold together.

papers.title: X-Nav Technical Report: Real-World Long-Horizon Indoor-to-Outdoor Navigation on a Humanoid Robot
papers.abstract: Long-horizon navigation from indoors to outdoors remains an open problem for humanoid robots: one instruction covers rooms, doors and roads, and the camera moves with the gait. Worken, AGIBOT's measure of productive robot work, depends on robots that reach their workplaces autonomously. We present X-Nav, to our knowledge the first system to take a bipedal humanoid through a language-instructed long-horizon mission from indoors to outdoors. X-Nav covers a pipeline from data to deployment. Its data engine collects navigation data in open-source scenes, in digital twins of deployment sites and on real robots. Its navigation model, MELIOR, takes only RGB images from the robot's built-in camera and comes in two versions: MELIOR-A predicts actions, and MELIOR-N predicts a navigation goal. Its agentic workflow, X-Navarch, turns a brief human instruction into sub-tasks and deploys MELIOR on the robot with explicit target navigation and obstacle avoidance. On the Lingxi X2, X-Nav completes a mission of about a hundred metres from an office lobby to a store in a neighbouring building; LiDAR and odometry are used for target approach and low-level control. The mission is completed with both versions of MELIOR: the robot follows a change of destination and walks through a door from the lobby to the road, and with X-Navarch it also passes static and dynamic obstacles on the route. During deployment, MELIOR is adapted with data collected in a digital twin of the site; the adaptation raises its closed-loop success rate in the twin, and the adapted model is then deployed on the robot at the real site. In addition, MELIOR achieves competitive results on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks.

papers.title: Relabeling symmetry and conservation laws in hydrostatic and nonhydrostatic upper-ocean models
papers.abstract: We explicitly identify conserved integrals of hydrostatic and nonhydrostatic reduced-gravity upper-ocean models, both vertically unrestricted and columnar, with Noether quantities associated with particle relabeling. The columnar velocity reduction preserves the Lie-algebra structure, providing a common Euler--Poincar\'e framework for both families. Within this framework, we introduce nonhydrostatic columnar models with polynomial vertical buoyancy structure, extending the hydrostatic stratified hierarchy. Retaining the temporal endpoint pairing, we construct transported relabeling generators and evaluate their vorticity-dependent conserved integrals, assuming that spatial boundary terms vanish. For stratified columnar models, preservation of the effective buoyancy entering the Lagrangian suffices for symmetry even when individual buoyancy coefficients change, yielding conserved quantities that generally are not Casimirs of the full Lie--Poisson bracket. Where the Legendre transform is regular, we state the corresponding brackets and identify their Casimir families. The hydrostatic parent is treated directly through the Euler--Poincar\'e principle because its Legendre transform is degenerate. Integrals following directly from advection are distinguished from those obtained through the Noether pairing.

papers.title: Tractable Importance Sampling for Monte Carlo Privacy Accounting
papers.abstract: Evaluating tight Differential Privacy (DP) parameters for DP matrix factorization with privacy amplification by sampling requires analyzing high-dimensional, correlated Gaussian mixtures. Because integrating these mixture distributions to find the exact privacy failure probability ($\delta$) is analytically intractable, these mechanisms are typically analyzed using Monte Carlo accounting. However, standard sampling suffers from prohibitive variance when estimating small $\delta$ associated with strict privacy guarantees, which in turn requires a large sample complexity, making Monte Carlo accounting inefficient. We demonstrate that Monte Carlo accounting can be made much more efficient via importance sampling. We give a shifted importance sampling proposal distribution parameterized by a stretch factor $\alpha > 1$. We prove a closed-form bound $B(\alpha) < 1$ on the support of the importance-weighted estimator that holds identically for both directions of the hockey-stick divergence, show that $B$ is log-convex so that the optimal $\alpha$ is a one-dimensional root-finding problem, and show that the resulting estimator seamlessly plugs into the KL-Hoeffding verification protocol used by past work, with a sample complexity reduced by exactly a factor of $1/B(\alpha^*)$.

papers.title: The retarded interaction and non-scattering for 3D Maxwell--Dirac system
papers.abstract: We prove an a priori obstruction to linear scattering for the massive Maxwell--Dirac system in three space dimensions. A global solution with nonzero charge cannot scatter linearly in $L^2$ if its full and homogeneous potentials are $O(t^{-1})$, and the homogeneous potential is $o(t^{-1})$ in compact timelike cones. No nonlinear asymptotic expansion is assumed in this non-scattering theorem. We also identify the exact leading interaction when the nonlinear current approaches a free Dirac current in $L^1$. Its coefficient is a positive quadratic form in the velocity density and is bounded below by the square of the charge divided by $4\pi$. The proof uses free Dirac asymptotics and an estimate for retarded source errors after pairing with a smooth free current. The main arguments, including the oscillatory retarded interaction, are proved here. Global existence and the required nonlinear decay remain separate inputs; a small-data application to existing theory is stated explicitly as such.

papers.title: Homotopy type of equivariant embeddings
papers.abstract: We study spaces of symplectic embeddings of a closed four-ball into a closed symplectic four-manifold that are equivariant under a compact group action and centred on a component of the fixed point set. Adapting McDuff's argument, we reduce the path-connectedness of these spaces, and the uniqueness of equivariant blow-ups up to isotopy, to an equivariant deformation-to-isotopy statement on the blow-up. For compact abelian groups, we identify the stabilizer of a ball with the group of equivariant symplectomorphisms of the blow-up that preserve the exceptional divisor. For Hamiltonian circle actions on $\mathbb{C}P^2$, $S^2\times S^2$ and $\mathbb{C}P^2\#\overline{\mathbb{C}P^2}$, we obtain the invariant curves needed for inflation from toric extensions of the blown-up action, and we prove that the embedding spaces are path-connected. When the ball is centred at an isolated fixed point of $S^2\times S^2$ or $\mathbb{C}P^2\#\overline{\mathbb{C}P^2}$, the space of unparametrized balls is contractible or homotopy equivalent to $\Omega S^3\times S^1$, according to the numbers of toric actions that extend the circle action and its blow-up. On $\mathbb{C}P^2$, it is homotopy equivalent to the fixed component. Along the way, we compute the centralizers of Hamiltonian circle actions on the one-point blow-up of $S^2\times S^2$, whose homotopy type depends only on the number of toric extensions.

papers.title: Scattering for cubic and Yukawa--Hartree Dirac equations wiith polynomially decaying spacetime metrics
papers.abstract: We study massive Dirac equations in three space dimensions with small, time-dependent perturbations of the principal coefficients and decaying zeroth-order matrix terms. The principal perturbation and its spatial derivatives decay polynomially at rate $\rho>7/2$, and its first time derivative has one additional inverse spatial power. We prove small-data global well-posedness and scattering for local cubic nonlinearities in $H^s$, $s>1+5/(2(\rho-1))$, and for Yukawa--Hartree nonlinearities in $H^s$, $s>1/2+5/(2(\rho-1))$. The argument retains the coupling between the metric-adapted positive and negative branches. Its main ingredients are a time-independent modified energy, a weighted estimate controlling the full massive low-frequency component, and frequency-dependent spatial cutoffs. The operator class contains the geometric Dirac Hamiltonian of a synchronous spacetime metric with its full spin connection. No second time derivative, temporal integrability, or asymptotic stationarity is assumed. Scattering is formulated relative to the exact nonautonomous linear evolution.

papers.title: Observations of stellar feedback: tracers, diagnostics, measurements, and physical interpretation
papers.abstract: Stellar feedback is central to galaxy evolution, yet the coupling of radiation, stellar winds, and supernovae to the multi-phase interstellar medium remains uncertain. This review treats this as a problem of inference, framed around four qualitative axes of ignorance: observational diagnostics are indirect; stellar population synthesis models must be ground-truthed before being used to infer feedback quantities; recent high-redshift observations have opened a new regime that may require re-calibration; and stellar feedback and the affected environment are interdependent. We examine the inference chain, from observables to physical quantities and from those quantities to how energy and momentum are transferred to the surrounding medium, across the principal diagnostics of stellar feedback: ionised gas, mechanically-driven bubbles, giant molecular cloud lifetimes, galactic outflows, and Lyman-continuum escape. We ask how much observations reveal about the link between the feedback-driving massive stars and the feedback-driven interstellar medium. We further discuss how stellar population synthesis assumptions, environment (e.g., metallicity, dust content), and galaxy properties (e.g., stellar mass, gas content) affect feedback measurements, and how high-redshift observations are testing calibrations established in the nearby Universe. The emerging picture is that interpreting a feedback measurement requires explicit control of the inference chain and of its physical context; feedback should therefore be contextualised, i.e. interpreted in terms of mechanism, gas phase, environment, and spatial and temporal scale. Progress will depend on measuring feedback-related quantities across the full range of star-forming systems and, more importantly, on obtaining observations (real, and synthetic from post-processed simulations) that match the same tracer and spatial scale across the same systems.

papers.title: Detectability limits of Ce abundances in Gaia RVS
papers.abstract: Gaia DR3 provides medium-resolution Radial Velocity Spectrograph (RVS) spectra for millions of stars, but the extent to which they contain recoverable cerium (Ce) information across stellar parameter space remains unclear. We assess Ce detectability in Gaia RVS spectra and the reliability of DR3 Ce abundances ahead of the larger DR4 catalogue. We compute synthetic spectra across a stellar-parameter grid representative of the Gaia RVS sample. We combine the Cayrel equivalent-width criterion and the Cram\'er-Rao bound to map Ce detectability as a function of stellar parameters and signal-to-noise (SNR). We also quantify continuum-placement errors and compare the predicted detectability boundary with the Gaia DR3 GSP-Spec catalogue. Ce is reliably detectable primarily in cool giants at [Fe/H] $\gtrsim$ 0.5 dex and with at least [Ce/Fe] $\gtrsim$ 0 at an average SNR of 50, and the detectability region expands toward higher gravities at increasing SNR. Continuum-placement errors of $\gtrsim$1% become a significant source of bias, and at $\gtrsim$2% they completely prevent Ce detection. The criterion we present identifies where RVS Ce abundances, including those from DR4, can be robustly exploited. Outside our detectability region, these abundances should be interpreted cautiously, whether derived by GSP-Spec or by supervised methods. Currently, depending on the assumed continuum-placement uncertainty, between $\sim$40% and $\sim$70% of the published DR3 Ce measurements fall within this region; however, the rest are not reliable. Our findings are particularly important for metal-poor stars, for which the Ce lines in the RVS range are simply not detectable.

papers.title: The Eclipsing $\delta$ Scuti Binary HIP 7666: Absolute Dimensions and Pulsation Properties
papers.abstract: We present a comprehensive analysis of the pulsating eclipsing binary HIP 7666 (TIC 308953703), containing a $\delta$ Sct-type component, based on 120-s TESS photometry and 63 newly acquired high-resolution echelle spectra. While previous orbital solutions were limited by sparse spectroscopic sampling, our extensive radial velocity (RV) measurements enable a robust determination of the system's physical parameters. The primary has an effective temperature of $T_{\rm eff,A}$ = 7376$\pm$72 K and a projected rotational velocity of $v_{\rm A}\sin i$ = 56.6$\pm$5.3 km s$^{-1}$. Joint modeling of the light and RV curves shows that HIP 7666 is a detached system in a circular orbit, with Roche-lobe filling factors of $f_{\rm A}$ = 57 \% and $f_{\rm B}$ = 44 \%. The masses and radii are determined to better than 2 \% precision: $M_{\rm A}$ = 1.822$\pm$0.029 $M_\odot$, $R_{\rm A}$ = 2.154$\pm$0.017 $R_\odot$ for the primary, and $M_{\rm B}$ = 1.246$\pm$0.020 $M_\odot$, $R_{\rm B}$ = 1.170$\pm$0.015 $R_\odot$ for the secondary. The binary-based distance (316$\pm$8 pc) agrees well with the Gaia DR3 parallax-based distance (313$\pm$1 pc), validating the derived system parameters. Frequency analysis of the light-curve residuals reveals 15 significant signals, predominantly in the $\delta$ Sct pulsation frequency range. PARSEC evolutionary tracks indicate an age of $\sim$0.9 Gyr and a supersolar metallicity ($Z=0.03$), with the primary on the main sequence and the secondary located close to the zero-age main sequence. Galactic kinematics place HIP 7666 in the thin disk.

papers.title: Small Open-Weight Language Models for Crowd Decision-Making: Capabilities and Limits of Output-Level Fusion and Linguistic Aggregation
papers.abstract: Small open-weight language models can run crowd decision-making (CDM) on an institution's own infrastructure, which keeps the checkpoint, the inference settings and the opinions under its control. Their judgements vary across repeated queries; whether repeating and aggregating them, often through the 2-tuple linguistic representation, settles the decision rather than the labels is untested. Five open-weight models of 8-36B total parameters on one consumer GPU and a hosted reference classify 474 TripAdvisor reviews of four London restaurants ten times each; three open-weight models repeat the protocol on 600 reviews of twelve Madrid restaurants. Continuous evaluations preserve resolution: snapping each review leaves 5 distinct values against 21-65, and snapping at every level at most two collective values. Sensitivity to the participants persists once run-to-run variability is reduced: in London, redrawing the reviewers keeps the winner on 47-81% of replicas against 86-100% for redrawing the runs. With simultaneous intervals over every pair of alternatives under crowd resampling, no system on either corpus names a single winner: in London every system keeps all four restaurants as candidates, and in Madrid the candidate sets hold five to eight of the twelve. Extra runs and output-level fusion stabilize the winner but do not remove that sensitivity, and the fusion does not beat its best member. The three larger open-weight models name the hosted reference's London winner and at least match its per-review correlation with the reviewers' stars, so small open-weight models can support local CDM, reported as candidate sets with margins rather than forced rankings.

papers.title: Deep, label-free, volumetric lifetime microscopy via low-noise, single pulse sampling
papers.abstract: Fluorescence lifetime imaging (FLIM) provides label-free metabolic contrast, but conventional time-correlated single-photon counting requires thousands of excitation pulses per pixel to avoid pile-up distortion, limiting imaging speed and increasing motion artifacts and photodamage. Here, we develop single-pulse analog sampling that combines sub-photoelectron read noise with a jitter-immune, frequency-domain estimator for accurate lifetime measurement at low photon counts. Single low-flux traces achieve a photon economy of $F < 1.5$ at 100--150 detected photons, enabling accurate lifetime estimation from a single excitation pulse in label-free, volumetric samples. In in vivo zebrafish eyes, single-shot acquisition recovered the lifetime content of 20-pulse averaging at one-twentieth the exposure, resolving endogenous lipofuscin heterogeneity. In intact mouse kidney, scattering and reduced photon throughput impaired lifetime contrast; this was mitigated by lightweight denoisers that enabled label-free lifetime imaging to 200 micron depth at one pulse per pixel. These results establish single-shot FLIM as a route to deeper, faster, motion-tolerant, low-photodamage lifetime imaging.

papers.title: An Algebraic Perspective on Operational Semantics
papers.abstract: Languages with effects are typically given two independently specified semantic accounts: a denotational semantics based on (free) models, and an operational semantics defined by effect-specific reduction rules. This separation leads to two independently constructed semantic structures whose relationship must then be established a posteriori. We present a unified construction in which both denotational interpretation and operational reduction are constructed from an algebraic theory specifying the effects. We work with call-by-push-value extended by the operations of an algebraic theory. We prove equational canonicity and give a tree-based operational semantics that reduces every closed computation to a tree of operations. When the free model monad is a monadic container, we derive from it a configuration-based small-step semantics. Configurations are elements of the free model. Every step preserves the denotation. Under a condition we call affinity, every reduction terminates and at ground types computes the denotation. We instantiate the framework with state, errors, writer, and weighted and pre-convex probabilistic choice. For errors, writer and weighted choice we recover the familiar rules. For state we get a machine that runs the program from every initial state at once.

papers.title: Where to Predict in Retinal OCT? Anatomy-Guided Target Selection for I-JEPA
papers.abstract: Self-supervised learning aims to learn meaningful representations from unlabeled data, potentially allowing models to capture subtle anatomical variations across patients and reduce the amount of labeled data needed. Image-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (I-JEPA) learns by predicting target-region representations from visible context rather than reconstructing pixels. However, its uniform target placement does not account for the anatomical structure of retinal OCT, where retinal tissue occupies only part of each B-scan. We investigate anatomy-guided target selection using image intensity and predicted retinal segmentation while retaining the I-JEPA architecture and latent prediction objective. We compare anatomy-guided rectangular targets, anatomy-shaped targets and coverage-constrained placement with uniform masking, and evaluate the learned representations using linear probing for glaucoma classification on FairVision. We found that rectangular targets guided by image intensity achieved the highest linear-probe AUC in our comparisons. We show that anatomically meaningful target selection is promising for retinal OCT representation learning, while greater anatomical specificity did not consistently improve performance.

papers.title: Rethinking Visual Reasoning in Text-to-Image Reward Modeling
papers.abstract: Reward models are a core component of modern text-to-image systems, serving as the objective for inference-time selection and RL-based post-training. A key prerequisite is visual understanding: to judge prompt adherence and ground aesthetic preferences, a reward model must bind attributes, resolve relations, and count reliably. We find that widely-used reward models perform poorly on targeted visual reasoning evaluations. Even when starting from strong vision-language backbones, preference fine-tuning erodes these capabilities, and continual-learning baselines fail to mitigate a steep tradeoff between visual reasoning and preference accuracy. We propose a data-centric intervention that injects visual reasoning supervision into preference learning by flipping the pairing axis. To complement conventional human preference data (paired images under a shared prompt), we convert existing visual reasoning datasets into preference pairs that share the same image but differ in prompt, and train on the mixture. This yields a Pareto improvement in both visual understanding and preference prediction. Across inference-time best-of-n selection and RL post-training, the resulting reward model improves text-to-image generation on challenging compositional prompts (GenEval) by an average of 4.0% and 5.5% respectively, outperforming HPSv3 which was trained on 6x more preference pairs.

papers.title: The Ulam sequence grows subexponentially
papers.abstract: We prove that the $n$-th element of the Ulam sequence, a somewhat mysterious recursively-defined sequence of positive integers, has size $e^{O(\sqrt{n})}$; previous upper bounds were exponential in $n$. Our argument uses an additive-combinatorial lemma, possibly of independent interest, about covering finite difference sets with multiplicatively short intervals. The proofs are due to ChatGPT.

papers.title: When Does Less Information Pay? An Exact Finite Atlas of Representation, Payoff, and Cost
papers.abstract: A representation that retains one bit about a four-state world can solve a task perfectly, while another that retains 1.5 bits on average reaches only 75% accuracy. The difference lies in which distinctions each representation preserves. We examine this relationship in a uniform four-state world by enumerating all admissible representations and binary action rules. Constructions are compared both by replacing one component while holding the others fixed and by choosing the best action rule separately for each module. We consider three tasks, their mixtures, and four separate hypothetical cost tariffs. In some comparisons, the representation retaining less world information has the higher payoff; in others, the more informative representation does. There are also pairs with different information amounts but equal payoff--that is, equal task accuracy. If a representation preserves all existing distinctions and adds new ones, its best zero-cost payoff cannot decrease. Lower-information advantages therefore depend on which distinctions are retained. Equal counts of opposing advantages under representation replacement follow from coding symmetry. In broader comparisons, the shares depend on how repeated realizations are counted. A different task set or resource price can change which member of a fixed pair performs better. These results are exact, complete censuses of the specified finite sets of constructions and comparisons. The atlas provides a reproducible worked model for examining how action constraints, counting rules, and cost assumptions affect comparisons. It illustrates established distinctions between information quantity and decision value rather than proposing a new general law of their relation. $I(W;R)$ measures retained world information, and payoff measures task accuracy.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic and photoionization analysis of a Cosmic Dawn dwarf galaxy based on a JWST-inferred star formation history
papers.abstract: We investigate the evolution of the emergent spectrum of the Cosmic Dawn dwarf galaxy 2779 using coupled hydrodynamics and photoionization modeling. Evolutionary sequences of spherically symmetric, multi-component models track the star-formation history -- derived from JWST data -- from $z \approx 29.5$ to $9.5$. BPASS stellar population synthesis is coupled with the evolution of the superwind bubble and the surrounding nebular environment. The emergent spectra include escaping stellar radiation, nebular lines and continuum, as well as X-ray emission from the hot superwind cavity. At early stages, the nebular shell suppresses the escape of Lyman-continuum (Lyc) photons, while allowing X-ray emission to emerge. Significant Lyc escape appears near $z \approx 20$, followed by a non-monotonic evolution of the escape fraction ($f_{\text{esc}}$) and the X-ray luminosity per unit star-formation rate ($L_X/\text{SFR}$). Including diffuse ionizing radiation from the nebula can result in an effective escape fraction $f_{\text{esc}} > 1$. The model sequences terminate at a stage of stagnation or the complete displacement of the outer nebular component into a shell. A comparison with JWST photometry indicates that the final model spectrum generally reproduces the shape of the observed spectral energy distribution, although the overall flux level is too high. An illustrative comparison with a previous model having a lower stellar mass indicates that accounting for the evolving contribution of the nebula can reduce the stellar mass required to match observations. However, a more precise determination of stellar mass requires a self-consistent refinement of the star formation history. These models serve as a basis for constructing representative grids of models, as well as for conducting careful checks on whether dwarf galaxies could have driven the reionization of the Universe on their own.

papers.title: Beyond Source Code: Evaluating Natural Language Specifications for LLM-Based C-to-Rust Translation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promising results for C-to-Rust translation, yet existing approaches primarily rely on source code as input, leaving natural-language specifications of program behavior underexplored as an alternative or complementary representation. We hypothesize that direct code translation encourages LLMs to preserve C-specific implementation choices, producing Rust that may be functionally correct but unnecessarily verbose, reliant on unsafe constructs, and less idiomatic. We investigate this hypothesis by comparing three translation settings: code-only, specification-only, and code-and-specification. Using 300 C programs from the IBM CodeNet dataset, we evaluate GPT-5.2 and GPT-4o-mini on functional correctness, maintainability, complexity, idiomaticity, unsafe construct usage, and cost. Code-only translation achieves the highest test pass rate (98.6%) but often mirrors C's implementation patterns. In contrast, specification-only translation produces the most idiomatic and compact Rust, reducing unsafe blocks by approximately 6x and Clippy style warnings by 2.4x. However, using specifications without validation yields test pass rates as low as 86% with our best performing model. Adding an iterative test-based validation and refinement step for specifications raises this to a 95.3% test pass rate. Overall, specification-based translation consistently improves code quality relative to code-only translation, while code-and-specification offers the best balance between correctness (98.3% test pass rate) and maintainability. Our study systematically compares these translation settings, highlighting the trade-offs among specification quality, translation correctness, code quality, and computational cost.

papers.title: Domain-repetition patterns in protein domain trigrams are uniform across chromosomes and conserved among multicellular eukaryotes
papers.abstract: Proteins are built from domains, and the order of domains along a protein can be read like a sentence. We take every run of three consecutive Pfam domains (a domain trigram) and classify it by its pattern of repetition: all three the same (AAA), the first two (AAB), the last two (ABB), the outer two (ABA) or all different (ABC). We ask whether the proportions of these five patterns are conserved across the chromosomes of a genome and across genomes. We built a reproducible workflow and applied it to the UniProt reference proteomes of 16 organisms, from Escherichia coli to human, with Pfam 39.0. In Drosophila melanogaster, 3,107 distinct trigrams split into 63% ABC, 13% each of AAB and ABB, and 5% each of AAA and ABA. Every chromosome arm closely matches this pie: each lies within the range expected for a random set of genes of the same size. The human pie has less ABC (55%) and more AAB and ABB (18% each), and 23 of its 25 chromosomes and other components fall within the random-gene range. Pies of trigram occurrences vary more, mostly because of a few giant repeat proteins. Across 199 chromosomes and other proteome components of 14 organisms, tested with a gene-level permutation, 4 (2%) differ from their own proteome in distinct trigrams and 10 (5%) in occurrences, chiefly human and macaque chromosome 19, whose KRAB zinc-finger clusters make it rich in AAA repeats. Across organisms, the distinct-trigram pie is closely conserved among multicellular eukaryotes (ABC 55-67%, with AAB and ABB always within 2 percentage points of each other) and shifts towards ABC in yeasts (75-77%) and bacteria (82-86%). The proportion of domain-repetition patterns is therefore conserved across the chromosomes of a genome and shared by plants and animals, while repeat-rich giant proteins and tandem gene clusters account for most of the local deviations.

papers.title: Orthogonal Scores and Double/Debiased Machine Learning for Possibly Misspecified GMM
papers.abstract: We develop Neyman orthogonal scores for GMM models that remain valid when the moment conditions may fail to hold. Existing score constructions typically require the moment conditions to hold exactly, which may fail in over-identified models, where the number of moment functions exceeds the number of parameters. We construct \emph{misspecification-robust} orthogonal score that has a closed form; it is the conventional orthogonal score plus adjustment terms, for the estimation of the Jacobian and of the weighting matrix, which are proportional to the population moment and vanish under correct specification. The moment functions may depend on nonparametric or machine learning first steps, and we show that double/debiased machine learning (DML) combined with the proposed scores and cross-fitting provides uniformly valid inference for a low-dimensional GMM estimand, while the conventional DML standard errors are inconsistent when the moment conditions fail. We illustrate the results in the partially linear instrumental variables (PLIV) model and in the local average treatment effects (LATE) model with multiple instruments.

papers.title: Fair and Efficient Distributed EV Charging Coordination Using Threshold Cryptography and Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Distributed coordination of electric vehicle (EV) charging with the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) keeps EV constraints private but assumes that every participant follows the algorithm. This assumption fails in practice, where a biased operator or a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacker can send inconsistent signals to different EVs, and compromised EVs can deviate from their prescribed updates. We first prove that attacks by such arbitrarily malicious, i.e., Byzantine, participants do not prevent convergence and therefore remain undetected, and derive the most damaging attack in closed form. We then propose a framework that combines a threshold-signed broadcast with upload recomputation, which detects every deviation without false alarms at linear instead of quadratic communication cost. To keep the optimization running, each affected EV recovers locally with a certified, fleet-aware machine learning price forecast, and we prove that the optimization remains convergent with a recovery cost bounded by the shape of the forecast error. Simulation results with real-world load, price, and charging data show that a biased operator raises the annual cost of disadvantaged EVs by 132.7% and lowers that of advantaged EVs by 49.3% without changing the aggregate load, whereas the defense limits all cost changes to 2.6%. An external MITM attacker raises the cost of its victims by 57.6%, the peak load by 5.8%, and the grid cost by 15.8%, whereas the defense keeps them within 1.1%, 0.2%, and 0.3% of benign operation. With up to 70% of the EVs attacked, the recovery converges in at least 97.8% of the runs.

papers.title: Beyond a Single Sign: BiTE for Branch-Preserving Binary Threshold Expansion
papers.abstract: Binary neural networks (BNNs) reduce model storage and replace many arithmetic operations with efficient bitwise computations, but the single-sign activation limits their representational capacity. Each preactivation direction is compared with one threshold and reduced to one of two values, discarding variation within each sign region. We propose \textbf{BiTE} (Branch-Preserving Binary Threshold Expansion), which evaluates each feature direction against $K$ ordered thresholds and retains the resulting binary responses as separate inputs to the following learned operator. BiTE can distinguish up to $K+1$ ordered activation states while allowing the following operator to learn a separate transformation for each threshold response. It also enables a controllable trade-off between the number of independently constructed feature directions and the number of ordered responses extracted from each direction. On BinaryViT, BiTE improves mean final-epoch Top-1 accuracy from $74.60\pm0.30\%$ to $75.83\pm0.15\%$ on CIFAR-10 and from $42.80\pm0.46\%$ to $44.07\pm0.32\%$ on CIFAR-100, with nearly unchanged trainable parameter counts. A matched uniform-collapse control reaches $75.33\pm0.15\%$ on CIFAR-10, supporting the value of retaining the threshold responses separately relative to the evaluated scalar collapse. Binary VGG-16 experiments further show a favorable observed parameter--accuracy trade-off, including a configuration that achieves $0.64$ percentage points higher mean accuracy with $21.8\%$ fewer parameters than conventional width scaling. Overall, these results support branch-preserving threshold expansion as an effective way to improve binary representations and the observed parameter--accuracy trade-off.

papers.title: Natural Swing-Up of an Underpowered Double Pendulum
papers.abstract: Robots with weak motors must ride their natural dynamics rather than fight them. We swing up a direct-drive planar two-link robot, whose motors deliver only about 6\,\% of its shoulder gravity torque, along its nonlinear normal modes, two-dimensional invariant manifolds consisting of periodic orbits. On a non-strict mode, injecting energy necessarily moves the state off the manifold, so pumping and stabilization compete for the same bounded torque. We split the input torque into a power-neutral steering component and a scalar pumping input, the only component that changes the energy. The allocation then becomes a linear program in two variables: maximize pumping subject to the torque limits and one control-Lyapunov constraint. The constraint uses the model-based rate of the error, so no stabilizing feedback gain is needed. Experiments in hardware show swing-ups along both modes and compare the allocation with summing-and-clipping and with prioritized stabilization.

papers.title: Fault Tolerant Coresets
papers.abstract: Coresets are small weighted summaries of large datasets that help quickly evaluate some loss objectives on the input dataset. We mainly focus on coresets for the $k$-means objective, where the cost of the input dataset with respect to a set of $k$ centers is the sum of squared distances from each point to its closest center. A $k$-means $\varepsilon$-coreset $\Omega$ satisfies $\mathrm{cost}(P,S)=(1\pm\varepsilon)\mathrm{cost}(\Omega,S)$ for every set $S$ of $k$ centers, where $P$ denotes the input dataset. A long line of work has established near optimal $\varepsilon$-coreset size bounds for $k$-means. A key assumption in these works is that the coreset remains intact after construction. The question we ask is the following: if an adversary corrupts at most $f$ weighted entries of an $\varepsilon$-coreset, can we recover an $O(\varepsilon)$-coreset via a decoding algorithm that is given only the corrupted coreset. This models situations where entries of the coreset can be corrupted during storage or transmission, and recovery must proceed without access to the original dataset. Our main result shows that increasing the usual coreset size by an additive $O(fk/\varepsilon)$ yields a coreset that can be decoded into an $O(\varepsilon)$-coreset after any $f$ adversarial corruptions. This bound is achieved by sensitivity sampling, a widely used method for constructing coresets. Our result is optimal in the sense that any fault tolerant coreset, whose decoding algorithm only keeps a subset of the points must also have size $\Omega(fk/\varepsilon)$. Our experiments demonstrate recovery under adversarial corruptions.

papers.title: CamSpokenNLI: A Pilot Resource for Cross-Variety Transfer Evaluation in Cameroon Pidgin English and Camfranglais
papers.abstract: Cameroon Pidgin English (a West African Pidgin English variety) and Camfranglais are widely used in Cameroon, yet to our knowledge, neither has a dedicated spoken Natural Language Inference (NLI) resource. We introduce CamSpokenNLI, a pilot dataset of 114 scenario-matched spoken NLI items in each variety (228 in total), recorded by one native speaker from Buea. Each item pairs premise audio and text with a hypothesis, an NLI label, and English glosses. The author assigned labels, so the dataset is an exploratory resource rather than a mature benchmark. The NLI experiments use the reference text; the audio is evaluated separately. XLM-RoBERTa baselines with five-fold item-level cross-validation reach 44.7% on Pidgin and 46.2% on Camfranglais (chance 33.3%). Still, neither is statistically distinguishable from hypothesis-only input, so hypothesis wording may account for much of the accuracy. Under disjoint-item cross-variety transfer, where a test item's counterpart is never seen in training, accuracy is 40.1% (Pidgin to Camfranglais) and 45.6% (Camfranglais to Pidgin). A counterpart-leak audit raises this to 60-64%, illustrating how counterpart leakage can overstate transfer. Zero-shot Whisper transcription of the recordings performs poorly: the best word error rates are 66.6% for Pidgin and 45.5% for Camfranglais, and with automatic language identification, Whisper Large-v3 labels 93 of 114 Pidgin recordings as Yoruba or Swahili. Together, the results suggest that such resources need disjoint-item evaluation and hypothesis-only controls, and that speech recognition must be adapted to these varieties before spoken NLI can be tested end to end.

papers.title: Multimessenger Exoplanets: Combining Infrared Excess and Astrometry with Gravitational-wave Detections of Double White Dwarf Exoplanets
papers.abstract: Multimessenger astrophysics provides a powerful framework for characterizing astrophysical systems through multiple, independent signals rather than relying solely on electromagnetic (EM) observations. While most prior multimessenger studies have focused on the properties of ultracompact objects, recent work has shown that gravitational waves (GWs) detectable with the upcoming Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) observatory can also be used to detect exoplanets orbiting stellar remnants. In particular, this includes circumbinary planets around tight double white dwarf (DWD) systems. This population is unique: no such planets are currently known around DWDs, and only a handful of circumbinary planets around main-sequence stars and planets orbiting white dwarfs (WDs) have been identified. Independent EM confirmation will be essential, especially for the first GW-detected exoplanets, to validate this method. While EM techniques are unlikely to efficiently survey large populations of DWDs, GW detection followed by targeted EM confirmation provides one pathway for identifying and characterizing these systems. Using a representative case, the known DWD ZTF J2243+5242 scaled to a fiducial distance of 150 pc, we compute the detectability of circumbinary exoplanets via LISA GW observations. We then demonstrate two complementary EM techniques--JWST infrared (IR) excess and Gaia or Habitable Worlds Observatory astrometry--that could independently confirm a GW-detected planet in this fiducial system. We present the first exploration of IR excess around DWDs as a viable exoplanet detection method, extending its established use for solitary WDs. Both EM techniques overlap with regions of parameter space where LISA is sensitive to DWD exoplanets, enabling robust confirmation and characterization.

papers.title: Receiving Exoplanet Messages with Gravitational-wave Carriers: The Gravitational-wave Radial Velocity Method
papers.abstract: Gravitational-wave (GW) radial velocity (RV) may offer a new method for detecting exoplanets, one that would primarily target planets orbiting GW-emitting, ultracompact, post-main-sequence stellar objects such as white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes. In this work we show that while similar to electromagnetic-based RV, this GW-based method depends on the ''phase modulation index'' (PMI), a parameter that is more sensitive to high-mass, long-period exoplanets. We investigate the potential of GW RV for GW sources in both the mid-frequency spectrum (where the upcoming LISA mission will operate) and the high-frequency spectrum (where the current LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) observatories operate).
