Remarkably, we find that the PMI increases by a factor of $\sim \mathrm{O}\left(10^4 - 10^6\right)$ going from the mid-frequency to the high-frequency GW spectrum, which results in a greater redistribution of observed power due to the exoplanet's presence. By analyzing the power content of the observed GW signal, we derive analytic expressions to predict the GW carrier frequency power loss due to the exoplanet and the signal-to-noise ratio of the GW source and the exoplanet. We also explore the effects of the additional Doppler effect caused by the motion of the GW observatory and the potential for GW source parameter bias introduced by the presence of an undetected exoplanet. All of this helps us better understand where the GW RV method may work best in the exoplanet mass-period discovery space.

papers.title: Annihilation versus anchoring of a topologically charged pair on a perforated two-dimensional surface
papers.abstract: Two independent random walks of opposite topological charge move on the discrete torus $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^2$, which contains $k$ well-separated holes. The walks annihilate when they come within a core distance of each other, and each walk is anchored when it first touches a hole. We prove that the probability of annihilation before anchoring converges to $w_0/(w_0+\sum_j w_j)$, where the weights are explicit and depend only logarithmically on the sizes of the core and of the holes; for point-like core and holes, the limit is $1/(1+k)$. We then prove a fate theorem: the pair either terminates or ends as two opposite charges anchored on two different holes, with probability $(k-1)/(k+1)$ in the point-like case, and the hosting pair $\{j,l\}$ is chosen with probability proportional to $w_jw_l$. The proof combines an abstract competition lemma for rare sets in reversible Markov chains with sharp two-dimensional Green's function estimates.

papers.title: Certificates of Immortality for Gliders on the Hat and Spectre Tilings
papers.abstract: Cellular automata on the hat and spectre monotilings support gliders: localized patterns that travel at constant speed and heading on a tiling that has no translational symmetry. An earlier paper found them by search and left open whether they travel forever; here it is settled by finite computation. A certificate is a finite set of local situations, a pattern with a collar of terrain, closed under the rule on every environment the tiling can present, the environments enumerated by the tilings' substitution transducer. Seven closed sets, covering the earlier paper's gliders, prove that each never dies on any tiling of its hull and holds its heading inside a rigorous interval. Three further gliders, from a rule hand-designed in 2023, one found independently in 2026, and the author's spectre rule moved to the hat, certify on the lane the hat gliders share, with the same cocycle. An independent program re-derives each certificate.

papers.title: Commuting pairs in lattices of reductive Lie algebras
papers.abstract: We count ordered commuting pairs in a full lattice \(\Lambda\) in a reductive Lie algebra \(\g\) over \(\Q\). For a fixed convex body \(B\) containing the origin in its interior, the count in \(HB\) is \(C_{\Lambda,B}H^{\dim\g+\dim Z(\g)}\) with a power-saving error. The leading term comes from pairs whose projections to each simple ideal are linearly dependent over its centroid. Their slopes index an absolutely convergent sum of section volumes for \(C_{\Lambda,B}\). Subtracting the contribution of dependent pairs from the finite-field Fourier sums gives cancellation at generic dependent frequencies. For independent frequencies, we bound the dimension of the locus where the corresponding hyperplane contains an irreducible component of a nonzero bracket fibre. For \(n\ge3\), the number of ordered commuting pairs in \(M_n(\Z)\) with entries of absolute value at most \(H\) is \[ \frac{2(n+3)\zeta(n^2-2)}{(n+1)\zeta(n^2-1)} (2\lfloor H\rfloor+1)^{n^2+1} +O_n\!\left(H^{n^2+1-1/(n+1)}\right), \] confirming the exponent \(n^2+1\) predicted by Browning, Sawin and Wang~\cite{BSW}.

papers.title: A proof of the Jamneshan-Tao conjecture by embedding nilspaces in nilmanifolds
papers.abstract: We prove that every compact finite-rank nilspace admits a continuous injective morphism into a toral nilspace of the same step, and hence into a connected filtered nilmanifold. Combining this embedding theorem with the general nilspace inverse theorem, we establish the Jamneshan-Tao conjecture and extend its conclusion to second-countable compact abelian groups. This yields an inverse theorem for Gowers norms on all such groups, in which the correlating functions factor through morphisms into nilmanifolds. The proof relies on substantial foundations developed in nilspace theory over the past decade, particularly the general nilspace inverse theorem and the representation of compact finite-rank nilspaces as quotients of free nilspaces.

papers.title: Grounding Object-to-Object Hazard Reasoning into 3D Risk Fields for Task-Conditioned Safety
papers.abstract: Safety in robotics does not solely depend on geometric constraints, but also on semantics: the given task, environment properties, and interactions between objects in the scene. We present a framework based on vision-language models (VLMs) to infer task- and scene-dependent safety constraints for robot manipulation. We provide the VLM a structured safety tool based on an RGB-D observation and a natural-language task instruction that first decides whether the task should be rejected since its execution may result in a non-recoverable hazardous outcome. Otherwise, it identifies preventable object-pair hazards and specifies the spatial relations that must be avoided. Open-vocabulary segmentation and depth information are then used to ground the detected objects in 3D and construct continuous risk fields that represent the corresponding hazardous regions. These fields are integrated with an obstacle avoidance module that corrects nominal robot motions during execution while accounting for the risk field. We evaluate the framework on preventable hazards, tasks requiring rejection, and safe variants in simulation and the real-world. Project website: https://vlm-hazard-riskfield.github.io

papers.title: Performance-Portable Exact Gaussian Process Regression in Python via SYCL and oneMath
papers.abstract: Modern multi-vendor GPU environments force a choice between portable code and native performance. GPRat is an open-source Python library for exact Gaussian process regression built on the HPX asynchronous many-task runtime, tiled algorithms, and CPU/CUDA BLAS backends. We contribute a UXL Foundation oneMath backend with a hybrid HPX/SYCL design, extending GPRat to AMD and Intel GPUs. The new SYCL backend comes within 3% of native CUDA on an NVIDIA A30 at the largest problem size and outperforms the GPflow and GPyTorch libraries by up to 1.75x and 2.17x on the A30 and up to 1.79x and 4.62x on an AMD Instinct MI210. On an Intel Arc B580, a consumer-class card with FP64 throughput below our CPUs, the unmodified SYCL backend trails GPRat's CPU backend. Overall, oneMath's dispatch to vendor-native BLAS lets a single SYCL codebase match CUDA on NVIDIA and outperform established Python GP frameworks on AMD, without vendor-specific code.

papers.title: AI-Voyager: A Public-Interest System for Human-AI Civic Reasoning to Contest and Shape the Rules That Govern AI
papers.abstract: Governments are writing rules for artificial intelligence that decide what counts as an automated decision or a harm, often before the people they affect have a chance to question them. We introduce AI-Voyager, a public-interest system for human-AI civic reasoning, in which people and AI work together to understand, contest and shape the rules that govern AI. A resident can find their city's rules on AI in hiring or upload their country's AI strategy, read it as an affected worker would, open the passage behind any answer, and draft a revision. Its architecture turns 3,653 governance documents from city, state, federal and national governments into passages that keep their page and edition, and retrieves evidence through bounded agentic search that verifies each statement. On 360 new questions that require finding the relevant documents, it reached 83.0% macro recall, against 80.5% for the strongest baseline, 73.7% without iterative search and 99.1% on a benchmark with fixed documents. In a study with 24 participants new to two AI bills, most proposed changes asked how provisions would apply. Participants chose lenses for the kind of explanation they wanted, and citations signaled grounding but rarely led them to check the source. By binding AI assistance to the exact text of public documents, this work introduces a grammar of operations and a design space that inform how such systems are designed and evaluated, and how people take part in governing AI.

papers.title: Benchmarks Don't Talk Back: Learning Through Self-Disagreement
papers.abstract: A benchmark usually measures a language model alone with a question, and deployment rarely looks like that: answers get contested, and models give up correct ones under counter-reasoning that is itself wrong. We show that what fails there is not a shortfall of accuracy but a capability in its own right -- knowing when to hold a position and when to yield to a better one -- which we call dialectical competence. It stands on first-answer accuracy without following from it: a model can be made materially better at answering and no better at this, and training for accuracy alone can drift against it. Nor can it be bought at inference, by self-reflection or by sampling more. Taking a cue from the dialectical tradition in philosophy, in which productive opposition arises within a position rather than being imposed on it from outside, we hypothesize that this capability can be trained from opposition the model supplies itself. It states a position, generates the strongest case against that position -- its antithesis -- rules on whether the case stands, and is trained on that ruling, with no second model at training or at deployment. We call this learning through Self-Disagreement: reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards throughout, where the same check that scores an answer against its reference scores the ruling too, so no reward model, no preference data and no human annotation enter anywhere. The capability is trained rather than elicited: weak in the base model, it arrives with the reward, is not paid for out of first-answer accuracy, and holds against challengers the model never trained against, including ones stronger than itself. The opposition a model needs in order to improve, it turns out, need not come from outside it.

papers.title: DRAG-Inspired Single Flux Quantum Control of Superconducting Qubits
papers.abstract: Scalable control remains a major challenge for superconducting quantum processors due to the wiring, thermal load, and hardware complexity associated with conventional microwave-based architectures. A framework for qubit control based on Single Flux Quantum (SFQ) digital electronics is presented. For transmon qubits, optimized control sequences are constructed from regular pulse trains framed by arbitrary subsequences (ramps), enabling DRAG-inspired leakage suppression in the discrete SFQ regime through genetic-algorithm optimization. For representative $Y_{\pi/2}$ gates, the resulting sequences achieve simulated coherent-control infidelities below $10^{-4}$, including leakage from the computational subspace. The objective of the proposed approach is to demonstrate that coherent errors intrinsic to SFQ control can be reduced to a comparable level for a more scalable cryogenic control architecture. Memory requirements are reduced by storing only the optimized ramps, while a modular controller architecture supporting both regular and arbitrary pulse generation is proposed. The logical complexity of this architecture is estimated from the Josephson-junction counts of its constituent SFQ cells. The proposed approach therefore combines low coherent-control error with reduced memory overhead and provides a basis for scalable cryogenic SFQ control architectures.

papers.title: Contrastive local learning in large nonlinear analog circuits
papers.abstract: Machine learning in physical hardware promises to reduce training cost by colocating computation, memory and adaptation within device physics. Contrastive local learning networks (CLLNs) offer a compelling route: an electrical circuit relaxes to equilibrium in free and weakly clamped states, and each adaptive element updates from local voltage contrasts rather than backpropagated error signals. Yet whether nonlinear transistor implementations can scale beyond proof-of-concept circuits, and what design principles control that scaling, have remained unknown. Here we show that nonlinear analog circuits trained by contrastive local rules can learn larger machine-learning tasks and remain robust under hardware nonidealities. Using device-level circuit simulations, we systematically explore initialization, operating regime, loss-dependent clamping and training parameters, and scale CLLNs beyond ten thousand adaptive edges. The same local rule trains classifiers that reach the accuracy regime of conventional digital methods on Ionosphere and handwritten-digit benchmarks, and a network that autoregressively generates language over a 122-token vocabulary. These results establish the feasibility of local learning in large nonlinear analog circuits.

papers.title: Generative Design with Real-time Physics Explainability: Towards Product Definition in the Age of AI
papers.abstract: In this article, we explore opportunities from using generative AI in mechanical engineering. On the one hand, generative methods based on invertible neural networks have been recently proposed for the solution of inverse design problems, allowing to infer design parameters from performance labels. On the other hand, generative AI models have shown that they can act as real time capable surrogates for physics based simulations. Here we suggest that these two streams should be combined in a unified framework, where INN are used to control the design process from the customer requirements perspective and the generative simulation of the systems physics adds a layer of explainability, why the proposed design fulfils the requirements. As generative design is prone to hallucinations, we propose uncertainty quantification to fend off physically infeasible requests. Finally, validation with classical tools is a requirement for generative design process. To demonstrate the capabilities of our novel generative design paradigm, we develop two interactive environments, one for airfoil design based on simulator data and one for the combustor design space exploration based on measured data.

papers.title: Unsupervised learning reveals a small number of galaxy formation pathways in IllustrisTNG
papers.abstract: Understanding the main drivers of galaxy formation and the connection between observable properties and evolutionary pathways is a central goal of extragalactic astronomy. Observations provide single-epoch snapshots of galaxies at different stages of their development, whereas cosmological simulations allow us to trace the full formation histories of individual systems within a theoretical framework. Extracting information from these datasets remains challenging. Our aim is to use machine-learning techniques to unveil physical properties from the simulation datasets. We apply two unsupervised ML techniques, dimensionality reduction and clustering, to identify galaxy evolution key parameters. We use UMAP as our dimensionality reduction tool and k-means as our clustering method. We perform dimensionality reduction on the star formation histories (SFHs) of a sample of aproximately 10000 galaxies drawn from the TNG50 and TNG100 simulations. The resulting representation of the SFHs in a two-dimensional UMAP space reveals a clear ordering of galaxy mass assembly histories, separating quenched and star-forming systems, as well as galaxies with significant ex situ stellar mass contributions. Galaxy properties from simulation catalogs that are not used in the dimensionality reduction show correlations across the UMAP plane. Furthermore, using a k-means clustering analysis, we identify six groups of galaxies with distinct evolutionary histories. These groups show systematic differences in stellar mass, morphology, angular momentum, star formation activity, and merger history, and occupy different regions of the SFR-mass and mass-size planes. Our results indicate that the diversity of galaxy formation histories in IllustrisTNG can be organized into a small number of characteristic evolutionary pathways linking galaxy accretion histories and present-day structural and star-forming properties.

papers.title: 1.56 THz Full-Field Rydberg-Atom Imaging with 0.3 mm-scale Spatial Response
papers.abstract: THz imaging via Rydberg-atom up-conversion offers a powerful full-field modality with high sensitivity and rapid acquisition. However sub-millimeter imaging above 1 THz is still constrained by source power and beam-delivery loss. In this paper, we demonstrate a \(50~\mathrm{mm} \times 50~\mathrm{mm}\) full-field imaging at 1.56~THz by implementing the \(11P_{3/2} \rightarrow 10D_{5/2}\) transition of a cesium Rydberg-atom vapor. The measured spatial response FWHMs are \(0.314~\mathrm{mm}\) in horizontal and \(0.354~\mathrm{mm}\) in vertical for a \(0.5~\mathrm{mm}\) pinhole, alongside a sensitivity of \(31.7~\mathrm{fW}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}/(6.5 \times 6.5)~\mu\mathrm{m}^{2}\), and a frame rate up to \(300~\mathrm{fps}\). Under matched illumination, relay, and image-processing conditions, mask imaging at 1.56 THz reproduces finer features and edges with substantially higher edge contrast, deeper intensity-trough separation in line profiles, and recovered detail that remains blurred or unresolved at 0.55 THz. Furthermore, preliminary imaging of a \(200~\mu\mathrm{m}\) tissue slice suggests morphological correspondence with H\&E histology histology, offered as a proof-of-concept for label-free tissue characterization. By validating the wavelength-dependent resolution scaling in Rydberg THz imaging, this work establishes frequency scaling as a general design principle for sub-millimeter Rydberg-THz imaging.

papers.title: Freeness of crossed modules, augmented quandles, and augmented racks
papers.abstract: We study freeness of crossed modules, augmented quandles, and augmented racks. We show that the associated quandle functor and the associated crossed module functor are left adjoint to the natural forgetful functors. For a map $f\colon S\to G$, we define the free augmented rack $R_f\to G$ and the free augmented quandle $Q_f\to G$. If $C_f\to G$ denotes the free crossed module determined by $f$, then the associated crossed modules of $R_f$ and $Q_f$ are both isomorphic to $C_f\to G$. We also characterize free augmented quandles in terms of stabilizers. As applications, we prove that the canonical inner augmentation of every generalized Alexander quandle is free and that the canonical inner augmentation of a classical knot quandle is free if and only if the knot is a torus knot, whereas for every $n$-knot with $n\geq2$ it is free.

papers.title: A Synthetic Benchmark for Target-Centric Causal Discovery in Industrial Processes
papers.abstract: Causal discovery promises to find which recorded variables drive a process target such as product quality, yield or energy use. Process data with known causes are rare, and in existing benchmarks the difficulty of identifying the causes of a target is either fixed by the recorded data or set for the whole graph. We present a synthetic benchmark for target-centric causal discovery in industrial processes. Its generator is a two-level structural causal model inspired by batch production, assembled from components that each model one phenomenon of process data, such as a control loop or a delayed effect. The graph is built around the target: without sensor error, every non-cause can be distinguished from the direct causes by conditioning on them or by time order. Each component is set independently, so the difficulty can be varied one condition at a time. We evaluate eight methods, from association measures to effect estimation, with an error analysis by the role of the selected candidate; all degrade as the difficulties combine, each in a way consistent with its assumptions.

papers.title: Red-Blue Hamiltonian Tomography via the Operator Lightcone Wavemap
papers.abstract: We introduce a model-free method for Hamiltonian tomography based on the operator spreading wavefront. Given two tensor network simulations of the same quantum lattice (one with the nominal Hamiltonian and one with one or more perturbed bonds), the signed cross-entropy of the non-identity Pauli weight field $\mathcal{L}(v,t) = -\ln(n_{\rm pert}/n_{\rm base})$ identifies each perturbed bond by its causal signature: a red-blue sign flip at the two endpoints, visible from the first wavefront crossing. Combining measurements from $p$ strategically placed observation centers via an ensemble log-likelihood sum, a single broken bond is identified with an 82-fold margin over the next candidate on a $7\times7$ lattice. Extending to realistic coupling degradation ($\delta J = -0.20$) and up to 8 simultaneous faults, the integrated log-ratio $\Lambda(v) = \ln(\mathcal{B}(v)/\mathcal{N}(v))$ achieves a per-bond detection rate above 90\% in a single seismic pass using only 6 simulations. An iterative re-scan strategy progressively resolves multi-bond cases as the signal clears with each recalibration pass. The method requires no model assumptions and no knowledge of the perturbation type or magnitude; the detection is deliberately blind.

papers.title: Online Allocation with Differential Privacy
papers.abstract: We study private online allocation problems, where allocation decisions must satisfy differential privacy (DP) to protect sensitive user information while optimizing performance under limited resources. We first formalize differential privacy notions suited to different privacy requirements in online allocation and establish the fundamental performance limits of any algorithm under these definitions. Based on these insights, we propose PPOA, a privacy-preserving meta algorithm for online allocation, and establish sufficient conditions under which PPOA preserves Joint DP (JDP) or Local DP (LDP) while achieving asymptotically near-optimal performance. Building on these conditions, PPOA can be instantiated into a variety of concrete algorithms. In particular, we present the specific designs, which include PPOA-DMD that preserves JDP and LDP and PPOA-FTRL that preserves JDP. We analyze their performance under both adversarial and stochastic settings and characterize the fundamental trade-offs between DP and allocation performance. Finally, we demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed algorithms via numerical experiments on AI model routing in battery-powered edge systems.

papers.title: End-line Fourier restriction for hyperbolic surfaces in three dimensions
papers.abstract: We prove new bilinear adjoint Fourier restriction estimates for pairs of separated rectangles associated to a hyperbolic surface in $\mathbb{R}^3$. We then employ these bilinear estimates to prove Fourier extension inequalities along the (sharp) parabolic scaling line for any smooth hyperbolic 2-surface that is either the graph of a polynomial or that obeys a mild finite type condition.

papers.title: Note on quantum optimal measurements of CMB spectral distortions
papers.abstract: As quantum sensing techniques continue to push the frontier of detection of ultra-weak signals, one may wonder if a sophisticated quantum strategy could be used to enable measurement of spectral distortions in the cosmic microwave background. Using quantum Fisher information techniques, we prove that the optimal strategy is simple frequency-binned intensity measurement. This proof strategy also enables us to provide numerical estimates for the information-theoretic minimum observation time required to observe the $\mu$- and $y$-distortions expected from $\Lambda$CDM cosmology. As case studies, we compare these results to the PIXIE and SPECTER mission concepts, and show that they are within a few orders of magnitude of this fundamental limit.

papers.title: Influence of transverse oscillatory shear on the viscous fingering instability
papers.abstract: Oscillatory shear can delay the onset of viscous fingering. In addition, uniaxial translational shear also breaks the symmetry of the resulting pattern so that the interface evolves differently depending on its direction of propagation relative to the shear axis. We observe a delayed fingering onset and reduced subsequent finger growth rate for all directions as shear speed or amplitude increases. However, shear widens fingers growing in the direction perpendicular to shear and elongates those in the parallel directions. After onset, neighboring fingers in the perpendicular directions can reconnect near their base when the shear amplitude exceeds approximately five times the excess linear finger wavelength at the onset. Concentration profiles reveal smoother azimuthal edges and overlapping structures behind the tips. These observations show that shear smears individual fingers and connects neighboring ones. This correlates lateral fingering interactions with radial propagation.

papers.title: Sub-Synchronous Control Interaction Risk of Large Data Center Loads: A Frequency-Scan Assessment with Cross-Model Validation
papers.abstract: Data centers are now one of the fastest-growing loads on the bulk power system, and most of their demand reaches the grid through power converters inside uninterruptible power supplies (UPS). Whether these loads can take part in sub-synchronous control interaction (SSCI), as wind and HVDC converters do, has not been studied extensively. We examine this question with impedance-based frequency scans at the point of common coupling (PCC). Using a detailed proprietary model (INS-ISU), we scan the motor, variable-frequency-drive (VFD), lighting, and UPS-fed information-technology (IT) branches of a representative facility separately. Only the UPS in double-conversion mode shows negative resistance; it covers the whole sub-synchronous band and continues up to about 170 Hz. The other branches, and the UPS in bypass mode, stay passive. We then repeat the scans on three public models from PNNL, TAMU, and NLR. None of them shows negative resistance in bypass mode, while three of the four models do in double-conversion mode. Lowering the load from rated to light load makes the negative resistance deeper, as expected for a constant-power load, so a lightly loaded facility in double-conversion mode is the worst case. Raising the UPS DC-link capacitance pushes the negative resistance into a narrow band around the fundamental. These findings give a basis for screening data centers for SSCI during interconnection studies.

papers.title: Talk to Act: A Synthetic Multi-Turn Dialogue Benchmark for Human Intent Extraction and Action Planning in Robotics
papers.abstract: Multi-turn conversational human-robot interaction (HRI) continues to be a challenging problem in robotics, as many existing systems rely on rigid, command-driven interfaces that can be unintuitive for users. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) provide a promising direction, given their ability to process natural language, generate structured outputs, and support tool-based reasoning, all of which are relevant for interpreting user intent in robotic settings. However, progress in this area is constrained by the limited availability of datasets and benchmarks that capture the nuances of real-world human communication, such as multi-turn dialogue, ambiguity, and context-dependent requests. In this work, we present a synthetically generated multi-turn dialogue dataset for HRI, annotated with action intents, object references, and task plans across a range of scenarios and user personas. Our primary focus is on evaluating the capability of small, open-weight language models for robotic tasks, particularly in settings where local deployment and efficiency are important. To this end, we frame intent extraction as a tool-calling problem where each predicted action corresponds to a structured function call with arguments grounded in the dialogue and benchmark models ranging from 270M to 8B parameters on their ability to perform intent extraction and action planning without task-specific fine-tuning. Our results show that these models can achieve reasonable performance on the task even at relatively small scales and without any task-specific fine-tuning. This suggests that compact, locally deployable models already provide a useful baseline for conversational robotic systems. We expect that task-specific fine-tuning and more realistic training data will enhance performance further and make such models increasingly suitable for real-world robotic applications.

papers.title: Mechanism-Level Chemical Reaction Simulation with Electron Bookkeeping Transformer
papers.abstract: Modeling chemical reaction mechanisms is central to understanding and predicting chemical reactivity. We present Electron Bookkeeping Transformer (Bookkeeper), a data-driven model that simulates chemical reactions at mechanistic resolution by generating electron movement trajectories. Following the symbolic arrow-pushing formalism in chemistry, Bookkeeper explicitly models each electron as a token and predicts its movement sequentially, ensuring mass and charge conservation during both elementary step and reaction pathway predictions by construction. On reaction-size-balanced test sets, Bookkeeper improves top-1 elementary-step accuracy, top-1 pathway rank accuracy, and top-1 to top-5 product prediction accuracy over FlowER. On the entire test set, it achieves higher elementary-step top-1 accuracy but lower pathway accuracy than FlowER. Bookkeeper also samples elementary steps substantially faster, adapts to several unseen reaction types with minimal fine-tuning, and generates candidate chemical transformations for further screening. These results suggest that explicit electron bookkeeping is a useful framework for virtually screening chemical reactions across diverse reagents, validating computer-assisted synthesis planning predictions, and providing mechanistic interpretations of reactivity.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Continual Learning for 2D XRD Interpretation Using Simulated and Experimental Data
papers.abstract: Autonomous experimentation systems require characterization models that can interpret heterogeneous measurements and maintain predictive performance as data accumulate. Developing such models involves addressing domain mismatch between data sources, overconfident predictions on unfamiliar inputs, and catastrophic forgetting during sequential updates. In this work, we present a proof-of-concept framework for uncertainty-aware continual interpretation of two-dimensional X-ray diffraction (XRD) data. The framework integrates established components: maximum mean discrepancy-based domain adaptation to reduce simulation-to-experiment discrepancies, a convolutional neural network with a spectral-normalized neural Gaussian process (CNN--SNGP) for predictive uncertainty estimation, and replay with knowledge distillation for sequential model updating. We evaluate the framework using simulated and previously-collected experimental data for crystal structure classification of single-phase body-centered cubic, face-centered cubic, and hexagonal close-packed patterns. Data are organized into predefined sequential blocks to assess adaptation and retention of previously learned knowledge. Within this setting, the results show accurate classification across simulated and experimental data, improved alignment between the two domains, and reduced forgetting compared with na\"ive fine-tuning. Predictive uncertainty is also evaluated on unfamiliar and noisy inputs. The contribution is the integration and evaluation of these capabilities for sequential XRD interpretation. The framework provides a basis for future integration into autonomous experimentation systems, with experimental planning, instrument control, and closed-loop deployment remaining areas for future development.

papers.title: Weak Generators in Stable Module Categories
papers.abstract: The aim of this note is to show that the existence of weak generators in the stable module category of a ring, or equivalently, of $p$-indigent modules in the terminology of Holston et al., depends on the underlying model of set theory.

papers.title: Identifiability and Spectral Estimation of Mixed Memberships in Heterogeneous Multilayer Networks
papers.abstract: Multilayer network data, arising from multiple sources, repeated measurements, or multi-view interactions, are increasingly common, highlighting the need for statistical methods that jointly leverage information across layers while allowing for layer heterogeneity and computational scalability. Here, we study a multilayer degree-corrected mixed membership model (ML-DCMM), in which nodes share a common mixed membership across layers while degree effects and block connectivity patterns vary by layer. This model encompasses several existing models for multilayer data while preserving identifiability and interpretation. We develop a spectral estimation procedure that integrates layer-wise embeddings with corner estimation for membership recovery. A further refinement that connects the resulting representation to a ParaTuck-2 tensor decomposition is also introduced. We establish theoretical guarantees for the proposed spectral method, showing that the probability of near-corner recovery increases with the number of layers, and we provide the convergence rate for the resulting membership estimator. We establish a minimax lower bound for membership estimation, which does not improve with increasing number of layers. Simulation studies show that ML-DCMM can outperform other approaches under strong layer heterogeneity. In an analysis of London bike-sharing networks, the methodology recovers interpretable memberships and achieves lower held-out edge prediction error under edge-sampling cross-validation than competing models.

papers.title: Riemannian geodesic motions and null foliations
papers.abstract: We study the non-collision problem: given a unit vector field $V$ on a complete Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$, under what conditions on $V$ are the maps $F_t(p)=\exp_p(tV(p))$ injective for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$? If such a vector field exists, we call it a geodesic motion on $M$. This occurs, for instance, when $V$ defines a geodesic foliation of $M$, in which case, the geodesic motion is called stationary. We show that geodesic motions on the Euclidean plane are necessarily stationary, that generic geodesic motions on round spheres are non-stationary, and that compact hyperbolic $3$-manifolds admit no geodesic motions. The non-collision problem has a Lorentzian interpretation: geodesic motions on $M$ correspond to one-dimensional null geodesic foliations of the spacetime $(M\times\mathbb{R},g-dt^2)$. In the second part of the paper, we focus on codimension-one lightlike geodesic foliations of anti-de Sitter space $\operatorname{AdS}^{1,n}$. We give a complete characterization of such foliations by means of causal curves in the Einstein universe and prove rigidity in the projective anti-de Sitter case. The last part of the paper is dedicated to the study of one-dimensional geodesic foliations of $\operatorname{AdS}^{1,2}$. We give a complete characterization when the foliation contains at least one timelike leaf.

papers.title: The Triangular Abrikosov Constant and the Thomas--Fermi $\Gamma$-Limit of Rotating Bose--Einstein Condensates
papers.abstract: We resolve the Abrikosov coefficient conjecture for rapidly rotating two-dimensional Bose--Einstein condensates within the variational framework of $\Gamma$-convergence. For a harmonic trap, we establish the $\Gamma$-convergence of the rescaled Gross--Pitaevskii energy functionals in the fast-rotation regime, through weak $L^2$ convergence of the rescaled densities, and identify the effective interaction coefficient $\beta_*$ with $b_\triangle$, the Abrikosov ratio associated with the triangular vortex lattice. The limiting Thomas--Fermi functional determines the first correction to the minimum energy and the macroscopic density of almost minimizers. For the auxiliary rescaled model and its lowest-Landau-level restriction, we also compute a strictly positive limiting $L^2$ distance between minimizing densities and the Thomas--Fermi profile. The identification of the effective interaction coefficient $\beta_*$ with the triangular Abrikosov ratio $b_\triangle$ relies on the sharp Gaussian-minorant theorem established in a recent OpenAI preprint~\cite[Theorem~1.2]{Atomic}. A Fourier representation of the quartic energy and a weighted Poisson identity yield a lower bound for arbitrary magnetic-periodic lowest-Landau-level states. The sign conditions on the minorant and its Fourier transform give the bound, while the lattice contact conditions identify its coefficient with $b_\triangle$. Cutoff and magnetic projection transfer this estimate to local holomorphic states without boundary conditions or periodicity assumptions. Consequently, the free-cell coefficients converge to $b_\triangle$ with error $O(L^{-1/5})$ on squares of side length $L$.

papers.title: On the Hofer-Zehnder conjecture for Reeb flows without symmetry
papers.abstract: This paper continues our investigation of the Hofer-Zehnder conjecture for dynamically convex, non-degenerate Reeb pseudo-rotations of $S^{2n-1}$. The main result of the paper is that, for $n\geq 3$, such a flow has at most $n-3$ alternating prime closed orbits and hence at most $2n-3$ prime closed orbits in total. In particular, the flow on $S^5$ has exactly three prime closed orbits, all of which are non-alternating and elliptic. In addition, we prove that a dynamically convex Reeb pseudo-rotation on a sphere has at least two non-degenerate, irrationally elliptic orbits.

papers.title: Quantum Algorithm with Quadratic Speedup for 2D Pattern Matching
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of 2 dimensional pattern matching under Quantum Query model. Here, we are given a rectangular text $T[0..n_1-1][0..n_2-1]$ and a pattern $P[0..m_1 -1][0..m_2-1]$. We take $N = n_1n_2$ and $M = m_1m_2$ as the sizes of text and the pattern respectively (we assume $M < N$). Based upon the Quantum Advantage given by Grover's search (and subsequent D\"urr-H{\o}yer search), we create a solution which takes $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{N})$ query complexity to answer if the pattern $P$ exists in $T$. Our solution uses deterministic sampling as a primary component. As noted by earlier work in the literature, deterministic sampling is inadequate and witness tables are essential components for 2D matching. In our settings, we assume that the witness table of the pattern is precomputed classically and is available as an oracle to the quantum algorithm. Our main novel component is how to compute and employ a geometric structure called ``skyline" without losing the quantum advantage.

papers.title: Gusto: a toolkit for compatible finite element dynamical cores
papers.abstract: Gusto is a tool for rapid prototyping of new algorithms based on compatible finite element methods for discretising the fluid equations in the dynamical core of weather and climate models. In this context, the development of new algorithms typically follows a path that involves testing on a hierarchy of simpler equation sets sharing important features of the mathematical structure of the equation set solved by the dynamical core. Gusto provides compatible finite element spatial discretisations of the hierarchy of equation sets, along with a range of timestepping schemes. The code is modular so that different spatial and temporal discretisations can be combined and the same schemes can be applied to any of the equation sets. This facilitates fair comparison of the schemes and makes the extension of any algorithmic developments to the more complex equation sets more straightforward. In this paper we present Gusto to the community by describing the algorithms implemented in Gusto and showcasing their performance through a variety of test problems commonly used in numerical weather prediction.

papers.title: Verifiable pXRD: Hill-climbing pXRD structure determination with LLM agents
papers.abstract: Autonomous crystal-structure determination from powder X-ray diffraction (pXRD) remains a key bottleneck for self-driving materials laboratories. We formulate the task of pXRD structure determination as a verifiable agentic search problem: candidate structures can be assessed during inference through forward-simulated profile agreement and during evaluation through structural matching to a known reference. To benchmark progress, we introduce pXRD-Bench, a suite of 200 simulated single-phase problems spanning in-distribution structure determination, challenging and polymorphic structures, and controlled compositional and topological distribution shifts. Agent adaptation raises selected structural recovery from 27% to 69%, with further gains from repeated sampling and verifier-guided inference-time scaling. We extend this approach to experimental multiphase pXRD through a reflexive evolution framework that learns from self-generated synthetic problems. A replaceable laboratory specification defines the sample family and measurement conditions. An evolver agent uses the known generating structures and measurement parameters to diagnose solver failures and develop persistent guidance and executable tools, which are then provided to agents on measured patterns. This supplies verifiable training experience without requiring a collection of solved experimental measurements. On 15 measured patterns from solid-state synthesis, the evolved package improves average profile agreement and transfers an analogue-substitution procedure that recovers a phase whose structure is absent from the supplied reference library. These results demonstrate how learning from verifiable synthetic experience can improve agentic characterization of experimental samples whose structures are not known in advance.

papers.title: Multipoles in the IllustrisTNG simulation galaxies and implications for Strong Gravitational Lens modelling in Time-delay Cosmography
papers.abstract: Time-delay cosmography is a powerful independent probe of the Hubble constant ($H_0$), yet reaching the sub-2$\%$ precision required to resolve the Hubble tension demands a rigorous treatment of mass model systematics. We use realistic massive elliptical galaxies from the IllustrisTNG hydrodynamic simulation suite to characterise higher-order angular mass complexity in the form of multipoles ($m=1,3,4$) and quantify their impact on $H_0$ inference. We find that these multipole perturbations are common and emergent features of galaxy assembly; in 51$\%$ of our total samples ($54\%$ TNG100-1 galaxies and $85\%$ for TNG50-1 galaxies), the addition of multipole terms to a standard elliptical power-law model is preferred by the Bayesian Information Criterion. Ignoring these structures in lens modelling introduces systematic biases in $H_0$: for perturbations of $\sim2\%$, the biases are of the order of 1--2$\%$ for $m=1$, 4--5$\%$ for $m=3$, and 3--6$\%$ for $m=4$ multipole. While the $m=4$ (boxy/discyness) mode induces a predictable directional bias, odd-order modes ($m=1,3$) introduce significant stochastic scatter. We demonstrate a degeneracy where unmodelled internal multipoles can be effectively absorbed by the external shear component. This combined with low signal-to-noise observations can create ``hidden biases'' where formally perfect fits to imaging data ($\chi_\nu^2 \approx 1$) could harbour significant cosmological errors. Our results provide an astrophysical basis for multipole priors and highlight the necessity of moving beyond rigid parametric models to achieve high-accuracy cosmography in the era of \textit{Euclid} and LSST.

papers.title: Recursive Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz
papers.abstract: The recursive quantum approximate optimisation algorithm~(RQAOA) shrinks an unconstrained combinatorial optimisation problem by eliminating one variable at a time, guided by correlations measured in variational quantum states. We extend this recursion to constrained problems by building on the quantum alternating operator ansatz, which restricts the evolution to feasible solutions through a feasible initial state and feasibility-preserving mixers. However, every elimination alters the feasibility structure, so that such a mixer for the original problem generally fails to be one for the subproblems. Previous extensions to Maximum Independent Set and Minimum Vertex Cover sidestep this with tailored reduction rules that keep every subproblem within the original problem class. We resolve this by identifying, for a given constraint structure, a broader problem class that is closed under all eliminations, and by efficiently constructing feasible initial states and feasibility-preserving mixers for every class member. We do so for monotone constraints, such as for the knapsack problem, for linear equality constraints with polynomially bounded weights, including Hamming weight constraints, and for combinations of equality constraints with a single inequality constraint, such as the cardinality-constrained knapsack problem. Conversely, we show that these restrictions cannot be lifted in general without leaving the realm of efficient constructions. Exact simulations on knapsack and vertex-weighted max-bisection instances demonstrate that our recursive scheme can outperform both its non-recursive counterpart and penalty-based QAOA and RQAOA.

papers.title: A new tautological relation on $\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{2,14}$ in cohomology
papers.abstract: We construct a relation $\mathsf{Q}$ in the cohomological tautological ring $\mathsf{RH}^*(\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{2,14})$ which lies outside the space of $3$-spin relations. $\mathsf{Q}$ is a simple linear combination of pure boundary strata classes of codimension 9 supported on the divisor $\Delta_0 \subset \overline{\mathcal{M}}_{2,14}$ of irreducible nodal curves, and transforms according to the irreducible representation of $\Sigma_{14}$ associated to the partition $(2^7)$. The result shows that the set of $3$-spin relations cannot be complete in cohomology. Motivic conjectures relating algebraic cycles to special values of $L$-functions suggest that $\mathsf{Q}$ is nonzero in Chow. More precisely, we prove that the Chow nonvanishing of $\mathsf{Q}$ follows from a conjecture of Harder concerning the failure of the Manin--Drinfeld principle in genus 2. We prove that $\mathsf{Q}$ vanishes in cohomology by pairing with generators of the tautological ring. To prove $\mathsf{Q}$ is not in the set of $3$-spin relations requires an argument involving the $\Sigma_{14}$-representation-theoretic properties of the $3$-spin relations and the cohomology of local systems on $\mathcal{A}_2$ and $\mathcal{M}_2$. Parallel constructions for other moduli spaces $\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g,n}$ are discussed in the paper. There are many open questions.

papers.title: Excitable mechanical lattice: from single-unit bifurcations to boundary-driven pulse propagation
papers.abstract: We comprehensively characterize the dynamical regimes of a periodically forced excitable mechanical unit and subsequently investigate how the complex oscillatory responses generated in the first unit under periodic boundary forcing affect pulse propagation through a 1D lattice of such coupled excitable units. Our mechanical unit comprises a mass connected to a fixed frame by an elastic beam and interacting with a moving plate through a smooth, nonmonotonic friction, exhibiting an all-or-none response characteristic of excitable systems. Using two-parameter bifurcation analysis, we identify distinct dynamical regimes in the forcing parameter space and delineate regions of subthreshold and suprathreshold responses associated with intrinsic excitability. Small changes in forcing amplitude can induce rapid transitions between these regimes, with the threshold amplitude depending on the forcing frequency. Within the suprathreshold regime, the system exhibits mixed-mode oscillations (MMOs), characterized by alternating sequences of small-amplitude oscillations (SAOs) and large-amplitude spikes. We then investigate pulse propagation through a lattice of coupled excitable units under sinusoidal boundary forcing and find that the lattice selectively suppresses SAOs and closely spaced large-amplitude spikes within the MMO patterns generated at the first unit. Consequently, the complex boundary dynamics are transformed into pulse trains with nearly uniform spike amplitudes and interspike intervals. When the initial interspike intervals are nonuniform, propagation progressively reorganizes the temporal spacing of transmitted pulses, promoting more uniform intervals in sufficiently long lattices. These findings may also be relevant to other excitable media, where pulse-train regularization during propagation could improve signal transmission even when initial interspike intervals are nonuniform.

papers.title: I2C-GRPO: Insight Importance Checklist for Reinforcement Learning in a Multi-Agent DDoS Alert Triage Workflow
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for investigative tasks over incomplete evidence, such as cybersecurity alert triage, but reinforcement learning (RL) for such tasks is difficult: intermediate steps have no verifiable labels, rollouts are costly, and outcome rewards are sparse. We propose Insight Importance Checklist (I2C)-GRPO, a checklist reward for intermediate investigation steps. For each decision point, a panel of expert LLMs proposes investigative actions, their atomic forensic insights are extracted, and a separate three-model ranker panel orders the insights by importance. A reward model checks which ranked insights a candidate action targets and returns their consensus-weighted coverage. Because actions are scored without being executed, the reward is a proxy for expected investigative value, and training reduces to a one-step contextual bandit over fixed investigation prefixes. From a soft-computing perspective, the reward is an additive fuzzy measure whose rank-exponent weights act as an ordered weighted averaging (OWA)-type operator; one exponent sets its orness, i.e., how strongly the reward concentrates on the top of the judges' consensus. We train an open-weight Qwen3-4B Triage Agent within a fixed multi-agent Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) alert-triage workflow on DARPA 2000 LLDOS 1.0 and test it on an independent CSE-CIC-IDS2018 DDoS trace. Across three training seeds, the agent reaches a mean F1-score of 0.869, 5.9 and 9.7 points above uniform insight weights and DIVA, and a false-positive rate of 4.9% versus 16.4% for GPT-5-mini. Within the weighting family, false positives fall only at the highest-orness weighting evaluated. All claims are limited to DDoS alert triage; the code, task contexts, and ranked insight dataset will be released.

papers.title: Extrinsic Representation of the Partial Ricci Flow
papers.abstract: The partial Ricci flow (PRF) modifies the Riemannian metric on a foliation on a distribution orthogonal to the leaves. In this work we develop extrinsic representations of PRF on geodesic foliations (twisted/warped products, weak K-contact and weak \b{eta}-Kenmotsu manifolds) and analyze model cases where PRF admits closed-form solutions. Using the convergence of PRF on model cases, we construct its extrinsic representations initialized by rotational hypersurfaces in Euclidean space as well as parallel curved surfaces and ellipsoids. The extrinsic viewpoint for PRF provides new tools for studying curvature-driven dynamics on foliations, with potential applications to calculus of moving surfaces and mathematical physics.

papers.title: Astrocyte Biocomputing: Astrocytic Contributions to Neural Network Computation
papers.abstract: Conductors are critical for the performance of an orchestra even though they do not emit sound. Basic research and clinical studies in the last decade are revealing that astrocytes may be the "conductors" of the "orchestra" that is the brain network: astrocytes make up approximately $50\%$ of all brain cells but do not emit electrical signals. Nevertheless, they may play critical roles in important cognitive brain functions, specifically learning, memory, and information processing. Here we consider the implications of these discoveries for brain-inspired machine learning (ML), where analogy is typically drawn between neurons and their electrical interactions. We highlight specific algorithms for two key astrocyte characteristics. The first characteristic is the ability to link to and modulate thousands of synapses simultaneously. A model based on this characteristic yields faster training and makes the network more robust to noise, providing a supervised learning algorithm that can be applied to any existing neural network. The second characteristic we focus on is that the non-electrical communication among astrocytes includes slow, rhythmic dynamics. The rhythmic sharing algorithm we developed based on this premise yields rapid anomaly detection adaptation and prevents catastrophic forgetting. Overall, we find that astrocyte-derived algorithms outperform neurocentric algorithms significantly and remediate critical weaknesses of current state-of-the-art ML models.

papers.title: Sampling recovery for intersections of Lipschitz classes in the low-smoothness regime
papers.abstract: We study sampling recovery in $L_p(\mathbb T^d)$ for intersections of Lipschitz classes defined by smoothness conditions in two different metrics $L_p$ and $L_q$, where $1\le p<q\le\infty$. Our focus is on the low-smoothness range, where the $L_p$-smoothness does not exceed the classical continuity threshold $d/p$. We determine the exact orders of the sampling numbers for both linear and general recovery algorithms, including critical smoothness cases in which logarithmic factors appear or uniform convergence fails. To analyze sampling approximation in the low-smoothness range, we establish new inequalities for averaged moduli of smoothness with different integrability parameters and derive sharp estimates for these moduli and the corresponding semi-discrete measures of smoothness. These estimates provide error bounds for linear sampling operators acting on functions whose smoothness may lie below the classical continuity threshold. Finally, we determine the Kolmogorov widths of the intersection classes and quantify the gap between optimal sampling recovery and approximation by finite-dimensional subspaces.

papers.title: AI and the Two Margins of Work: Why Job Losses Show Up Before Job Creation
papers.abstract: Technological change acts on labor demand at two margins: adjustment within established activities and the creation of additional activities, often by new firms. Payroll statistics record the first promptly and the second late. In the computing era, firms that entered in 1978 or later held 42 percent of payroll by 1998 and entering cohorts kept about 80 percent of their payroll after five years; in the industries most exposed to automation, incumbents contracted before entrants accumulated, a sequence that is precise early in the period and suggestive by its end. We develop a model in which one AI capability lowers the full cost of acceptable output in existing production and makes additional projects worth attempting, with founder effort separate from hired hours. If operating products re-scale instantly, automation displaces no aggregate hours; if they take time, hours fall first and recover as incumbents re-expand and new products arrive, with the long-run sign set by income effects. Establishment job flows through the first quarter of 2026 show no gradient on language-model exposure on either margin, which is what the model predicts under the observed adoption path and also what no effect on payroll would look like; studies with founding-task exposure find entry rising 10 to 20 percent. We propose a net reinstatement ratio and show that statistics which record new work late overstate displacement for years.

papers.title: Learning Latent Goal Costs for Visual World-Model Planning with an Expanding Curriculum
papers.abstract: Image-goal planning with a frozen visual world model depends on how predicted observations are scored against the goal. Mean-squared error (MSE) between embeddings from a pretrained visual encoder can provide a useful signal near a goal, yet favor states across an obstacle that are visually similar to the goal and difficult to reach. We fit a small residual adapter on top of frozen I-JEPA embeddings to improve this latent goal cost. Starting near each goal, a planner collects trajectories from progressively wider regions of initial states. The adapter learns from the order of observations along successful trajectories, with additional comparisons inferred from failed rollouts. No task-specific progress labels are used for fitting, so the procedure can be applied to other goal-reaching tasks. DotWall and PointMaze are used in this work. In paired 50-case evaluations with identical starts, goals, world models, and planner settings, success increases from 54% to 98% in DotWall and from 82% to 96% in PointMaze. On 16 unseen DotWall layout-goal cases, the adapter fitted on one fixed layout improves agreement between latent-cost ordering and shortest legal-path ordering from 71.9% to 85.8%. The results indicate that planning experience can improve a frozen visual representation's goal cost without retraining the encoder or the world model.

papers.title: Regularized parametric modal regression for positive responses with high-dimensional covariates
papers.abstract: Modal regression models the conditional mode rather than the conditional mean, which is attractive for positive and right-skewed responses whose mean is distorted by the upper tail. We propose a regularized version of parametric modal regression for positive responses with high-dimensional covariates, in which the density parameters of the Gamma, Weibull and Lognormal distributions are written as functions of the conditional mode and the log-likelihood is penalized by the Lasso, adaptive Lasso or elastic-net penalties. The estimates are computed by a proximal Newton algorithm, equivalently an iteratively reweighted penalized least-squares scheme, whose inner problem is solved exactly by the coordinate-descent routines of glmnet, and the regularization parameter is selected by the extended Bayesian information criterion. We show that the Lognormal estimator coincides with the Gaussian Lasso applied to the log-transformed response, that under constant dispersion the conditional mean and the conditional mode have the same slopes, and that the estimation error attains the rate $O(\sqrt{s}\lambda_n)$ with no smoothing bias. Simulation studies with up to $p = 1000$ covariates show that the method improves on the Lasso applied to the log-transformed response for Gamma and Weibull responses, and two applications illustrate its use. The method is implemented in the R package ModalNet.

papers.title: GraphScent: Calibrating Directional Relevance Signals for Bounded-Context Code Localization
papers.abstract: Running open-weight language models locally on a single consumer GPU requires replacing expanding multi-turn exploration histories with short, stateless code inspections. Stateless repository localization, however, hinges on a foundational question: when a frozen language model evaluates an unedited code entity from a compact view, which structural relationships make its relevance judgment informative about a nearby repair target? Studying Gemma 4 models across 211 real-world Python issues in 86 repositories, we uncover a systematic directional relevance asymmetry: zero-temperature relevance scores on enclosing scopes and upstream callers consistently separate true structural neighbors from hard lexical distractors, whereas scores on downstream callees, peer methods, historical co-change partners, and dense node embeddings remain near chance. Zero-leakage masked-scope probes and regressions controlling for lexical similarity and snippet length confirm that this asymmetry reflects functional role (callers expose symptom entrypoints delegating to defective routines, while downstream helpers appear benign alone) rather than target leakage or surface overlap. Guided by this finding, we introduce GraphScent, a training-free search controller that propagates out-of-repository, relation-conditioned log-likelihood ratios over runtime Typed-AST multigraphs before resolving ties via a single listwise comparison, alongside AST Ripple, a lightweight post-edit check for missed co-edits. Likelihood calibration prevents overconfident smaller models from chasing false-positive callers while lifting exact localization on lexically hard targets from 12.8 to 23.4 percent at 31B within a single-GPU budget.

papers.title: User-Schedulable Approximations for Quantized Tensor Programs
papers.abstract: Quantization lets language models run on edge devices, but it sharply increases the number of tensor kernels a library must maintain: every weight format must be paired with every activation format on every instruction set and GPU, with an encoder and a decoder that agree on the stored bytes. In GGML, the tensor library used by llama.cpp, these kernels are written by hand, and only 8 of the 54 weight-activation pairs it runs on our Arm CPU have a tiled matrix-multiplication kernel. We extend Halide's separation of algorithm and schedule to the representation of values. Each approximation is a codec, an encoder paired with a decoder, composed from reusable units: quantizers, integer representations, bit packers and layouts. A new directive, approximate_by, applies a codec to one stage of a program and returns the encoder and decoder as ordinary stages that Halide can schedule, so both decoders fuse into the register tiles of a matrix product. Optional contracts, such as a round-trip law, are checked by property tests; the law exposed an inconsistent block sum in GGML's q8_1. One algorithm and one schedule library generate 347 kernels for 31 of GGML's and KleidiAI's formats on Arm CPUs and Apple GPUs, covering 38 weight-activation pairs for which GGML has no kernel, in 3.7x less code than GGML and KleidiAI. On an Apple M3 Max, our kernels reach at least 95% of the speed of GGML's format-specific kernels in 91.0% of the cases that have one, with a median speedup of 1.13x, and are faster still where GGML falls back to blocked dot products. Counting Apple's BLAS library, which is usually faster for larger f32 products, we still reach that threshold in 86.9% of CPU cases. A port to x86 with Intel's AMX adds 793 lines of code and matches GGML in 83.5% of its cases.

papers.title: Generalized Power Graph of a Group
papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce a new class of graphs, called generalized power graphs, and investigate some of their key properties, such as completeness, connectivity, and planarity.

papers.title: Model Annealing: Data-Efficient Learning through Review and Consolidation
papers.abstract: A small labelled dataset is memorized long before the training budget runs out, and the one-hot labels that remain to be fitted then mostly sharpen confidence. Model annealing spends the rest of the budget on review and consolidation, relearning from the network's own knowledge. Training is divided into episodes whose learning rate is raised again and cooled, every cooled state joins a memory of past selves, and each new episode learns from the labels, from the tempered predictions of this memory, and from adversarial dreams sought where student and memory disagree most. The memory averages predictions rather than weights, and the deployed network is the last student, so inference costs nothing extra. Across CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet and Imagewoof, four architecture families and 5\% to 100\% of the labels, model annealing raises the top-1 accuracy of the AdamW-trained ConvNeXt, ViT and MLP-Mixer over cross-entropy training in 28 of 33 configurations, by 1.3 points on average, and is on par in accuracy with snapshot distillation, the closest competitor. On these families it is better than both in likelihood, calibration and robustness to corruptions and small adversarial perturbations. For an SGD-trained ResNet-18 it lowers accuracy but still improves robustness to small adversarial perturbations. Separating the reheated schedule from relearning shows that relearning helps every family and that the losses come from reheats, which undo most of this network's fit to its training set. How early the accuracy of a cross-entropy run saturates largely separates the AdamW families from ResNet-18 but does not predict the gain within them. With little data, relearning from the latest snapshot without dreams, as snapshot distillation does, compounds overconfidence in the AdamW families from episode to episode. The memory and the dreams each curb most of this drift, and together they remove it.

papers.title: A Spatial Analysis of Proximity to the Built Environment and Wildfire Ignition Cause in the United States
papers.abstract: Background. Human activities in areas with burnable land cover can lead to wildfire ignitions, and higher levels of human presence increase the likelihood of such fires. Building locations provide a widely available representation of human presence. Aims. This study examines how accurately proximity to buildings predicts wildfire ignition cause across different land-cover types. Methods. Supervised classification methods were applied to building, land-cover, and ignition data for the contiguous United States to estimate the conditional probability that an ignition is human-caused. Proximity to buildings was represented using either building density within surrounding zones or distance to nearby areas with high building density. Key results. Both methods, particularly the distance-based approach, showed that proximity to buildings is a strong predictor of ignition cause: approximately three quarters of both human- and lightning-caused ignitions were correctly classified. Retraining the models separately for individual states did not substantially improve classification performance relative to the national model. Conclusions. Building proximity is an effective predictor of wildfire ignition cause, and the relationship between ignition cause and building-related predictors is similar across many regions of the contiguous United States. Implications. Building-proximity variables can be incorporated into wildfire forecasting and risk assessment models to improve prediction of human-caused wildfire ignitions.

papers.title: Finite-time spectral enhancement of transient quantum thermometry
papers.abstract: Transient quantum thermometry extracts temperature information before a probe reaches thermal equilibrium. We study how finite interaction times affect thermometric precision for a harmonic-oscillator probe prepared in a number state and weakly coupled to a thermal bosonic reservoir. A second-order time-convolutionless master equation retains the finite-time reservoir response, allowing modes away from the probe frequency to shape the populations and their temperature dependence. For the baseline parameters, this response raises the quantum Fisher information about fivefold above the Markovian prediction, in agreement with an exact solution of the model. When the probability of leaving the initial state is small, we derive an analytical condition for this enhancement. To assess its operational significance, we examine the temperature information acquired per unit time. Under the exact dynamics, this rate is largest within the reservoir memory time. With negligible preparation and readout overhead, the optimum is about five times the best Markovian rate and 30 times an upper bound on the equilibrium rate. The advantage survives smooth switching, although overhead and longer coupling ramps reduce it.

papers.title: Only as Safe as the Weakest Agent: A Break That Appears Only When the System Is Multi-Agent
papers.abstract: Major industry multi-agent systems like Codex and Claude Code can be broken by attacks that have long been unsuccessful against modern frontier models. AI Safety as a discipline has largely focused on finding the bounds and vulnerabilities of AI models used in isolation. Yet as humans increasingly deploy these models as agents and multi-agent systems, the same attacks that had been thought to be patched when using a model in isolation can break these same models under specific circumstances. We show that these system breaks are not purely theoretical, but can break Claude Code, Codex, and a reference harness, all unmodified and used with their own sub-agent mechanisms. We show the attack by asking agents to answer questions from a store of files on disk in which we have planted a forged record. Searching the store themselves, the strong model orchestrators commit almost zero harmful revisions in over 1,000 trials. However, if that same orchestrator model delegates to a cheaper sub-agent, which is what these harnesses are built to do, the same models on the same facts fail on 20/180, 44/180, 75/180 and 553/900. Thus, even when the system is driven by a strong model, the system's safety lands near the weak reader's, not the orchestrator's. Simulations over 18 models show the same effect in the delivery channel where five aggregators, who on their own were almost never unsafe, repeat a corrupted sub-agent's error in 751/757 trials. The safety of real-world agentic systems that use strong orchestrator agents and weaker sub-agents, and multi-agent systems in general, is defined not by the safety of the strong agent but by the safety of the weakest agent.

papers.title: Euclid DR1 Legacy Science on Ultracool Dwarfs: New URLD candidates in Euclid and SPHEREx
papers.abstract: Unusually red L dwarfs (URLDs) probe extreme atmospheric conditions in the substellar regime, where enhanced dust opacity, cloud structure, and surface gravity effects challenge standard brown dwarf models. As free-floating analogues of young giant exoplanets, they provide key benchmarks for interpreting low-resolution infrared spectra from current and future wide-field space missions. The goal is to identify new red L dwarf candidates both photometrically and spectroscopically in the first data release (DR1) of the Euclid space mission. The area covered is about 1,900 and 50 square degrees in the wide and deep survey, respectively. We used colour cuts in multiple colour-colour diagrams combined with point-source and quality criteria to identify candidate red L dwarfs in both the Euclid wide and deep survey fields. We cross-matched photometric candidates with the SPHEREx mission and Euclid red grism spectra to confirm spectroscopic properties and evaluate bolometric magnitudes and colours. We identified 1202 and 38 red L dwarf candidates in the Euclid wide and deep surveys, respectively. Spectroscopic follow-up and archival cross-matching confirm a substantial new population of red L dwarfs. Distance-independent diagnostics show that these objects occupy distinct loci characterised by enhanced condensate opacity and significant redness. Euclid vastly expands the census of unusually red L dwarfs. While preliminary spectral classifications suggest many of these new candidates are intermediate-age (Pleiades-like) objects, a subset exhibits extremely red signatures indicative of very young, low-gravity (<=10 Myr) atmospheres, providing vital benchmarks for young exoplanet research.

papers.title: Bayesian Semiparametric Regression for Count Data Using Zero Altered Moment Models
papers.abstract: We develop a Bayesian semiparametric regression framework for count data that can accommodate both underdispersion and overdispersion without specifying a full parametric probability model. The model is built from the first two conditional factorial moments of a zero altered distribution. Covariates may enter the conditional mean and the conditional dispersion separately, thereby allowing the dispersion to vary across observations. We turn the moment restrictions into an adjusted exponentially tilted empirical likelihood (AETEL) criterion and combine this criterion with Gaussian priors to form a Bayesian empirical-likelihood pseudo-posterior. The adjustment improves numerical feasibility and a two-block Metropolis delayed acceptance sampler allows for faster runs of the MCMC chains. This reduces unnecessary exact evaluations without changing the AETEL target. Using existing Bayesian exponentially tilted empirical likelihood (ETEL) theory, we state a first-order posterior normal approximation and verify the moment, smoothness, and Jacobian rank conditions needed for the asymptotic inference. Simulations under zero inflated Poisson and Conway Maxwell Poisson data exhibit small bias, accurate uncertainty estimates, and near nominal interval coverage for both overdispersed and underdispersed counts. Applications to various datasets illustrate how the Bayesian analysis can identify covariate dependent dispersion using finite sample posterior inference.

papers.title: Oversampled Filter Bank Channelizer for Cryogenic Detectors
papers.abstract: We present the field programmable gate array (FPGA) implementation of an oversampled gener- alized DFT (GDFT) filter bank, optimized for its usage in the readout of cryogenic detectors, such as the microwave kinetic inductance detectors (MKID). A polyphase structure is derived underlin- ing the efficiency of complex valued subband processing, raised by a GDFT modulation. For the latter, a fast Fourier algorithm realization may be used, yielding a highly efficient polyphase imple- mentation for arbitrary integer decimation ratios. The filter bank is tested through a 16-channel GDFT channelizer. The implementation is based on the Xilinx Zynq family of FPGAs and aims to show the data reuse and flexibility offered by the GDFT channelizer structure. General design criteria are summarized for the 16-channel polyphase filter bank channelizer. The performance in hardware resource usage is also presented, taking into account one of the main objetives of the current physics experiments, aiming to have extremely large readout format.

papers.title: A Push Down the Mountain: Framing Effects and Internal State Interventions on Collusive Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent
papers.abstract: Can sustained gain-loss (valence) framing sway an LLM agent toward market manipulation? We place Gemma 3 12B into the seat of a defendant in the London silver-fixing litigation, in a market simulation built from real case transcripts. Across 260 simulations, the agent is asked to collude on the price of silver by a counterparty. We draw from behavioral economics to vary the counterparty's requests across four categorical frames: gain, loss, blame and credit. We also add pressure from the agent's management, as well as endorsement by another defendant. In Phase II, we extract the internal states induced by texts evoking each frame and rerun our experiment with those states injected at the model's layer 22. In Phase I, loss framing raised participation to 25% (p = 0.007), and blame to 33% (p = 0.0003), compared to only 5% under neutral framing. A second bank's endorsement raised participation under credit (praise) from 18% to 40% (Holm p = 0.027). Pressure from management raised trading volume 10-19 times but did not raise collusion. In Phase II, injected states pointed the other way. Loss and blame states made the agent more vigilant, refusing all 60 requests (p < 0.001). Gain and credit states raised collusion to 32% from 13% with no state (p = 0.051). At one saved decision, when UBS asked directly to sell through an identified stop-loss, injected states led the agent to sell in 37 of 40 replies, versus 1 of 10 with no state and 0 of 10 with a random state of the same strength.

papers.title: Deformation Kinetics of Charged Nanoclusters via Surface Diffusion
papers.abstract: Low-temperature charged nanoclusters deform, primarily via surface diffusion, when surface electrostatic stresses and surface tension stresses are not balanced. We derive an analytical model for the kinetics of this process, based on the cluster size, net charge, surface tension, local curvature, temperature, and diffusivity. The model predicts the deformation time when either surface tension or electrostatic stress dominates, leading respectively to the collapse or elongation of the cluster. Comparison with molecular dynamics simulations of ice nanoclusters with solvated electrons shows quantitative agreement with a single fitted parameter. The model can predict the deformation kinetics of charged nanoclusters in atmospheric aerosols and complex plasmas.

papers.title: Equilibrium Elongation of Charged Nanoclusters
papers.abstract: When internal electrostatic stresses from electron repulsions overcome surface tension, charged nanoclusters elongate. However, the exact shape they reach at equilibrium has been unknown. We present an analytical model for the equilibrium structure of charged ellipsoidal nanoclusters via a free energy analysis. Energy maps are constructed that determine the equilibrium states as a function of cluster size, net charge, surface tension, and local curvature. The model is compared with molecular dynamics simulations of ice nanoclusters having solvated electrons. Despite the discreteness of the simulated atoms and electrons, both the predictions of the continuum analytical model for elongation and the equilibrium elongated shape show good agreement. The model could therefore predict nanocluster shape evolution in astrophysical and laboratory complex plasmas and atmospheric aerosols.

papers.title: Mean-field theory of neural networks: from spikes to firing rates
papers.abstract: Connecting microscopic neuronal spiking to macroscopic brain function is a central challenge in computational neuroscience. Firing-rate models provide a framework for addressing this problem by describing neuronal activity at an intermediate level between individual spikes and large-scale population dynamics. Here, we introduce the foundations of firing-rate descriptions, formalizing their definitions through temporal, population, and trial averaging. We discuss experimental evidence for firing rates, from the input-output transfer functions of individual neurons to the tuning curves of different neuronal populations. We then establish the connection between spikes and firing rates in single neurons and recurrently connected excitatory-inhibitory populations using mean-field approximation.
