We illustrate how collective dynamics emerge from neuronal interactions, including population stimulus-response curves and bistability induced by recurrent coupling, and brain rhythms arising from synaptic depression. We briefly review extensions and applications of firing-rate models to learning, seizure-like oscillatory activity, visual selectivity, phase-amplitude coupling in neural oscillations, and whole-brain modeling. Together, these examples illustrate how firing-rate models provide effective descriptions of neural activity, linking the dynamics of individual neurons to collective computations across scales.

papers.title: Cartan Dynamics and Limit Sets on Flag Manifolds
papers.abstract: The classical convergence principle describes the collapse of the Riemann sphere under divergent sequences of M\"obius transformations. We develop its counterpart for arbitrary real semisimple Lie groups acting on flag manifolds, and use it to study limit sets and domains of discontinuity of discrete subgroups. The key is to let the source move: the destination of $x$ under $(g_m)$ is the set of all limits of $g_mx_m$ with $x_m\to x$. Our destination formula computes it as the closure of a unipotent orbit, determined by the Cartan data and a bounded Levi factor. The stratified convergence principle organises these destinations into families of translated Schubert varieties attached to boundary points of a compactification of the group. Over the complex numbers, the destination relation is the support of Brion's limiting graphs in the wonderful compactification, providing scheme structures, multidegrees and diagonal intersections. For discrete groups, the union of destination relations determines proper discontinuity and whether a largest domain exists. It relates Quint's flag limit set, Conze--Guivarc'h, Kulkarni and Myrberg sets to the recurrent set, while balanced choices of cells yield domains for every discrete subgroup, without Anosov hypotheses. For symmetric-power actions of non-elementary Kleinian groups on $\mathbb{CP}^N$, we compute the largest domain by a multiplicity bound at points of the classical limit set; for $N\ge3$ it strictly contains the Kulkarni domain, which equals the equicontinuity region. We also obtain nonempty largest domains for Zariski-dense cusped Hitchin groups with unipotent elements, and examples of strongly irreducible groups with no largest domain.

papers.title: Probing Spatiotemporal Quantum Correlations with Two-Qubit Relaxometry
papers.abstract: Quantum impurities and spin qubits are powerful local probes of magnetic fluctuations, but conventional relaxometry reduces their information to a local relaxation rate at a single frequency. Building on advances in two-qubit sensing of spatial correlations, we show how two complementary protocols probe finite-time correlations in interacting quantum matter. Phase-cycled Bell-state relaxometry isolates the signed contribution of correlated relaxation to the joint ground-state population. To second order in the probe-environment coupling, the resulting population contrast measures a finite-time integral of the energy-ordered cross-correlator. In the longitudinal regime, XY8 covariance probes the complementary symmetrized cross-correlator within a tunable frequency window. For a gapless quantum spin chain, the signals reveal interaction-dependent algebraic scaling and ballistic propagation. Luttinger-liquid theory links sign changes as the qubit frequency is swept to the propagation time between the probes. It also predicts distinct spatial power laws for the Bell signal before the correlation front and at late times, when the sensing window resolves the qubit frequency. Matrix-product-state calculations for the spin chain test the pre-front scaling at zero and finite magnetization and extract the propagation velocity from Bell oscillations at zero magnetization. The probe coupling geometry determines which spin and momentum sectors contribute to the measured signals.

papers.title: In-plane diffusion, spurious drift and a physics-structured gap predictor for a free colloidal pair
papers.abstract: When the diffusivity of a Brownian particle depends on position, its mean displacement acquires a noise-induced (spurious) drift whose magnitude is set by the stochastic convention $\alpha$. We ask how much of this physics can be extracted from a pair of 1.95 $\mu$m polystyrene spheres released from blinking holographic optical tweezers at five bath temperatures between 2 and 40 $^\circ$C. The single-sphere diffusivity inside the pair stays between 0.093 and 0.098 $\mu$m$^2$ s$^{-1}$, whereas the Stokes-Einstein value for water rises from 0.126 to 0.361 $\mu$m$^2$ s$^{-1}$; an isolated sphere reproduces the deficit, which is therefore not a pair effect. From the measured gap-dependent diffusivities $D_\parallel(h)$ and $D_\perp(h)$ we build a Fokker-Planck predictor of the future gap and score it on held-out releases. It recovers the 90% width of the gap distribution up to 800 ms but cannot discriminate between $\alpha = 0$, $1/2$ and $1$, because the $\alpha$-dependent mean shift is an order of magnitude smaller than that width. The ensemble spurious drift is consistent with zero at both ends of the temperature range, and the regression for $\alpha$ never exceeds $R^2 = 0.22$. We therefore present a planar methods baseline and identify the measurements required to resolve $\alpha$.

papers.title: Parametric Modal SARIMA Models with Skewed Distributions
papers.abstract: Seasonal autoregressive integrated moving-average (SARIMA) models typically target the conditional mean of a time series under a Gaussian error assumption. This approach may be inadequate when the innovations are asymmetric because the conditional mean no longer represents the most likely outcome. We propose the Modal SARIMA$(p,d,q)\times(P,D,Q)_s$ model, which links the conditional mode, rather than the conditional mean, to a multiplicative seasonal ARIMA structure. The innovations follow the Fernandez-Steel class of skewed distributions (SKD), whose location parameter is the mode, and the non-seasonal Modal ARIMA$(p,d,q)$ model is the special case without seasonal terms. We give the conditional log-likelihood for the Skew-Normal, Skewed Student-$t$, and Skewed Laplace members, establish the stationarity and invertibility conditions on the product polynomials, show that the recursive modal forecast is the joint mode of the future trajectory, and characterize the correction that yields the marginal $h$-step conditional mode. Monte Carlo experiments show that conditional maximum likelihood and its Wald inference are reliable when the seasonal factors are well separated, that the test of symmetry holds its level from about 200 observations, and that the modal estimator of the dynamic coefficients is as efficient as Gaussian least squares under symmetry and 1.2 to 2.6 times more efficient under asymmetry or heavy tails. We also show, analytically and by simulation, that nearly cancelling seasonal factors amplify the effect of the starting values, and that beyond one step the recursive forecast must be corrected to remain a forecast of the most probable value. In an application to the Canadian lynx trappings, a seasonal component for the ten-year cycle improves the non-seasonal fit for every member of the SKD family. The methods are implemented in the R package ModalForecast.

papers.title: Correlation distribution for a class of Niho exponents via self-conjugate-reciprocal polynomials and Kloosterman sums
papers.abstract: Let $q=2^m$ for an even $m\geq 6$ and let $d=s(q-1)+1$ with $4s\equiv5\pmod{q+1}$. In this paper, the correlation distribution between a binary m-sequence of period $q^2-1$ and its $d$-decimation is considered. The cross-correlation function takes seven values $q(i-1)-1$ for $0\leq i\leq 6$, and we determine their frequencies based on the study of low-degree self-conjugate-reciprocal polynomials and three mixed Kloosterman sums, which are finally expressed in terms of $K_m(1)$ and $K_m(\omega)$, where $K_m(\cdot)$ is the Kloomsterman sum on the finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ and $\omega$ is a primitive element of $\mathbb{F}_4$.

papers.title: Adversarial Tracking: Attacks on Image Sensors for Object Tracking in Autonomous Vehicles
papers.abstract: Object tracking systems estimate the motion of surrounding vehicles by linking detected objects across video frames. In particular, Tracking-By-Detection (TBD) systems combine object detectors with motion prediction and data association to maintain object identities over time. However, neural network-based detectors are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that perturb input images, and their impact on downstream trajectory estimation is not fully characterized by detection accuracy alone. Therefore, this paper evaluates image-specific and image-agnostic attacks on YOLOv3 and YOLOv4 detectors paired with SORT, Deep SORT, Strong SORT, and OC-SORT tracking systems. The evaluation uses CARLA simulator and measures tracking quality through Multiple Object Tracking Accuracy (MOTA), Higher Order Tracking Accuracy (HOTA), and Identification F1 (IDF1). Under image-specific attacks, HOTA for YOLOv3-based trackers declines from 53.45-56.19% to 14.85-17.03%, while MOTA reaches -772.60% in the worst case. YOLOv4-based trackers exhibit greater robustness, while HOTA still declines to 25.06-26.86%. In addition, image-agnostic attacks can reduce the tracking accuracy using a single Universal Adversarial Perturbation (UAP), without generating a separate perturbation for individual frames.

papers.title: Learning monotone game-theoretic linear MPC
papers.abstract: We propose a method to learn a game-theoretic model predictive control (GT-MPC) law by imitation from input and output data of a running multi-agent system. By interpreting the recorded inputs as the first moves of the equilibria of a game played by the agents, we learn the GT-MPC weights under hard input constraints and soft output constraints, without requiring the agents to reveal their objectives. We also impose that the resulting generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problem is strongly monotone, which ensures the existence and uniqueness of the equilibrium and, hence, that the learned GT-MPC law is well defined and can be evaluated efficiently online by variational GNE-seeking algorithms for linear-quadratic games. Moreover, strong monotonicity implies that the equilibrium is almost everywhere differentiable with respect to the references and the weights, which enables automatic differentiation for gradient-based optimization. In addition, we promote closed-loop stability of the unconstrained equilibrium feedback by incorporating a penalty that involves a jointly learned quadratic Lyapunov function. Learning a GT-MPC formulation enables us to explain the agents' objectives, reproduce their behavior in simulation in new scenarios, optimize their set-points, design mechanisms, and enforce additional constraints. A numerical example illustrates the approach.

papers.title: Multifidelity Operator Inference for Dynamical Systems
papers.abstract: This paper presents a multifidelity (MF) formulation of Operator Inference (OpInf) for learning non-intrusive, physics-based reduced-order models (ROMs) of nonlinear dynamical systems. OpInf learns reduced operators from projections of snapshot data by solving a least squares regression problem. However, generating high-fidelity snapshots can be computationally expensive, limiting parameter coverage and the temporal extent of training trajectories for many aerospace applications, which can lead to inaccurate or unstable ROM predictions. This work proposes MF-OpInf, which combines limited high-fidelity snapshots with more plentiful low-fidelity snapshots through a control-variates-inspired MF least squares formulation to learn a single set of reduced operators across multiple trajectories. Low-fidelity trajectories provide additional parameter coverage and extend beyond the high-fidelity training time horizon. The low-fidelity snapshots are also used to construct an improved reduced basis through weighted proper orthogonal decomposition. We demonstrate MF-OpInf on a nonlinear reaction-diffusion problem with parametrized sinusoidal forcing and a two-dimensional incompressible flow past a cylinder with a parametrized inlet pulse. In these experiments, under an equal training simulation budget, MF-OpInf reduces the mean relative prediction error at unseen parameters by up to $87\%$ for the reaction-diffusion problem and $28\%$ for the cylinder flow problem over the test time regime, which extends beyond the high-fidelity training time horizon. These results demonstrate that MF-OpInf can improve temporal extrapolation and prediction at unseen parameters without increasing the training simulation budget.

papers.title: Dual-Slack Frontier Matching: Parallel Approximate Maximum-Product Matching
papers.abstract: Maximum-product bipartite matching supports scaling and static pivot selection in sparse matrix preprocessing. We present Dual-Slack Frontier Matching (DSFM), a deterministic, shared-memory parallel algorithm for approximate maximum-product matching. Motivated by heavy matchings on small candidate supports, DSFM searches progressively exposed subgraphs ordered by fixed dual slack. Slack-ordered certified completion guarantees a perfect matching whenever one exists, or a maximum-cardinality matching with a Hall certificate otherwise. Every returned perfect matching carries an a posteriori geometric-mean quality bound; accumulated Hall obstructions can tighten this bound and improve the returned scaling. We compare DSFM with Heavy-Weight Perfect Matching (HWPM) and exact MC64 assignment on 598 nonsingular matrices. DSFM attains higher matching quality than HWPM over most quality thresholds. On a set of large instances consisting of 37 matrices, DSFM achieves a $3.53\times$ geometric-mean speedup over MC64, compared to $2.29\times$ for HWPM.

papers.title: Advancing Quantization for R&R Models with Microscaling Formats
papers.abstract: Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models, particularly in digital advertising, require massive inference throughput but exhibit extreme sensitivity to precision loss. Unlike Large Language Models (LLMs) that frequently tolerate quantization-induced accuracy drops of 1% or more, production-grade R&R models enforce a stringent launch bar: model quality must remain within a 0.01% Normalized Entropy (NE) margin relative to the baseline, which commonly uses FP16 or FP32. This tight constraint has historically hindered the adoption of aggressive quantization in this domain. In this paper, we present an empirical evaluation of both MXFP8 and the 6-bit MXFP6 format for industrial-scale R&R inference on the AMD MI350X architecture. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper, across R&R and LLM domains, that reports significant speedups from native MXFP6 GEMMs, which quantize both weights and activations and compute directly on 6-bit elements, without sacrificing model quality. We demonstrate that we can selectively apply this 6-bit format to maximize overall QPS gain without breaching the strict NE parity threshold. We further show that MXFP8 is a viable alternative to row-wise FP8: the two formats have nearly the same accuracy on our models, so the faster kernel can be chosen for each GEMM shape. On two production ads ranking models, our implementation shows measured GEMM kernel speedups over FP16 of 1.33--1.55x for MXFP8 and 1.73--1.99x for MXFP6 across all supported linear layers, and up to 2.90x for MXFP6 on individual layers, alongside end-to-end (E2E) inference throughput gains from selective MXFP6 of 1.5--5.3% for Model A and 7.6--14.3% for Model B over their FP8 configurations.

papers.title: Adversarially Batched Online Learning
papers.abstract: We introduce adversarially batched online learning, where the learner may update its decision rule only at a restricted set of time steps. Equivalently, the time horizon is partitioned into batches, within which the learner must use a fixed policy. We study this model for four canonical problems: stochastic bandits, online convex optimization, prediction with expert advice, and adversarial bandits. For stochastic bandits, we identify a universal complexity measure based on relative batch growth and establish both gap-dependent and gap-independent regret bounds. We show that the multiplicative penalty relative to the standard gap-dependent complexity can grow superlinearly in batch hardness. For the remaining three, we show that the optimal regret is tightly characterized by the 2-norm of the batch-length sequence. The upper bound is achieved by a batch-oblivious learner who does not know the batch structure, via a generic adaptive doubling trick tailored to this complexity measure. In contrast, the lower bound holds even for batch-aware learners.

papers.title: Continuous Cuffless Blood Pressure Estimation Using PPG From Methods to Clinical Translation
papers.abstract: Continuous blood pressure (BP) monitoring could improve hypertension management by capturing changes that intermittent cuff measurements miss. Photoplethysmography (PPG) is widely explored for cuffless BP estimation because optical sensors are inexpensive, wearable, and already present in many consumer and clinical devices. PPG, however, does not measure arterial pressure: BP is inferred from waveform characteristics or pulse timing, which also depend on vascular tone, arterial stiffness, sensor contact, motion, and individual physiology. This survey reviews PPG-based cuffless BP estimation along the full measurement chain, covering physiological mechanisms, waveform features, pulse arrival time (PAT), pulse transit time (PTT), machine-learning methods, datasets, calibration, validation, deployment, bias, and clinical translation. Studies are assessed by the strength of evidence they provide rather than by reported error alone, with particular attention to subject and temporal leakage, dataset imbalance, calibration dependence and drift, motion artifacts, and the gap between benchmark accuracy and reliable real-world measurement. The review finds that progress depends on more than better prediction algorithms. Future work should prioritize physiologically informed models, diverse longitudinal datasets, transparent reporting of calibration requirements and failure rates, stronger evaluation protocols, and studies that demonstrate practical value in clinical care.

papers.title: New Closed-Form Approximations in Statistical Mechanics Obtained by Symbolic Regression
papers.abstract: Obtaining accurate and analytically tractable closed-form expressions for complex physical systems remains a fundamental challenge in statistical mechanics. In this work, we investigate three approximation problems in polymer statistical mechanics using two complementary symbolic regression frameworks: Deep Symbolic Optimization (DSO), based on reinforcement learning, and PyOperon, based on genetic programming with nonlinear least-squares constant optimization. First, for the force-extension relationship of the Worm-Like Chain (WLC) model, DSO achieves a maximum relative error below 0.15%, while PyOperon reduces it to 0.05%, outperforming the Marko-Siggia formula (approximately 17%) and the Petrosyan approximation. Second, for the logarithmic factorial, ln(n!), both frameworks recover the dominant structure of Stirling's formula directly from analytical data. Using residual learning on a continued-fraction expansion of the Stirling remainder, PyOperon reduces the maximum relative error by a factor of 1.3 x 10^4 compared with the most accurate of nine classical approximations for n in [1, 30]. Third, for the non-Gaussian radial probability density of the Freely Jointed Chain (FJC) model, physics-informed residual learning improves the approximation by factors of 11.2 over Darabi et al. (2023) and 4.6 over the steepest-descent approximation. The discovered expressions remain analytically tractable across all three applications. These results demonstrate the complementary capabilities of DSO and PyOperon for discovering accurate closed-form approximations in statistical and continuum mechanics.

papers.title: The radical pair mechanism can generate nuclear-spin entanglement
papers.abstract: The radical pair mechanism is a quantum-mechanical process underlying weak magnetic field effects in chemical and biological systems. While nuclear polarization and electronic entanglement in this mechanism have been studied extensively, the possibility of creating entanglement between nuclear spins has, to the best of our knowledge, remained unexplored. Here, we show that nuclear-spin entanglement can develop from initially maximally mixed nuclear spin states and evolve over repeated radical pair cycles. Its generation and persistence depend on the initial electronic state, the available reaction channels, and the interplay between recombination rates, hyperfine interactions, and the magnetic field. We demonstrate this behaviour in both a minimal two-nucleus model and a five-nucleus model inspired by the photosynthetic radical pair P700--$A_1$. Radical pair mechanism generated nuclear-spin entanglement offers a potential new resource for quantum technologies and opens avenues for exploring its role in biological systems.

papers.title: Wasserstein geometry of analytic cycle spaces
papers.abstract: We use optimal transport to define an intrinsic distance on connected components of the Barlet space of analytic cycles on a compact K\"ahler manifold, by associating to each cycle its normalized volume measure. We prove that any two cycles in the same connected component can be joined by a deformation of finite Wasserstein length, and that the resulting metric is complete and geodesic. On the locus of smooth reduced cycles at regular parameter points, Wasserstein lengths and energies coincide with those of the normalized Weil--Petersson metric. The construction thus gives a transport interpretation of Weil--Petersson geometry and extends beyond it to components containing no smooth reduced cycles.

papers.title: An Operationalization of Opaque Serial Depth
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) is currently a valuable tool for overseeing AI models, but some architectural shifts could significantly reduce CoT monitorability. We operationalize a measure that serves as a proxy for the amount of unverbalized serial cognition a model can perform, as a specific instantiation of the notion of opaque serial depth: roughly, the length of the longest path through a model's computation that does not pass through an interpretable bottleneck. Our main contribution is a particular standard for what counts as such a bottleneck. We define natural-language-rooted (NL-rooted) nodes as nodes that were initialized from a pre-training prior to produce human-understandable outputs, whose output space has not been expanded beyond that prior, and whose outputs the model has not been modified to interpret as a different type of data. By construction, the resulting measure, NLS depth, can be adjudicated before training from an architecture, training recipe, and deployment configuration alone, and is insensitive to ordinary post-training such as prompting, distillation, and RL. We find that, across open-weight models, NLS depth correlates strongly with layer count, with some exceptions, and has grown slowly over recent years. It would likely grow slowly under continued scaling of standard transformers, while latent-reasoning architectures such as full-bandwidth transformers could increase it by a large amount. We work through how NLS depth applies to a range of existing and proposed architectures, discuss alternative operationalizations, and give a worked example bounding the depth of Gemma3-1B. We argue that AI developers should track and report the NLS depth of their models as a complement to direct measurements of CoT monitorability.

papers.title: New Congruences for Simultaneously $l$-Regular and $t$-Distinct Partition in $k$-Colors
papers.abstract: Let $RD_{\ell,t}^k(n)$ enumerates the number of $k$-colored simultaneously $l$-regular and $t$-distinct partitions. In this article, we establish some new infinite families of congruences modulo prime $p$, $p\geq5$ and modulo powers of 5 for $RD_{\ell,t}^k(n)$. For instance, for each $n\geq0$, $0\leq\alpha\leq{2k-2}$ and $k\geq1$, \begin{align*} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}RD_{(5^{2k-1},5^{2k-1})}^2\big(5^{2k+\alpha-1}n+\frac{9\cdot5^{2k+\alpha-1}-2\cdot5^{2k-1}+1}{12}\big)q^n\equiv& 0\pmod{5^{k+\left[\frac{\alpha}{2}\right]}} \end{align*}

papers.title: Noncommutative Rational Positivstellens\"atze with Operator Coefficients
papers.abstract: We establish a convex Positivstellensatz for noncommutative rational functions with bounded operator coefficients. A hermitian operator-valued rational function that is positive semidefinite on a matrix convex set described by a linear pencil admits a positivity certificate consisting of rational hermitian squares and a completely positive term involving the defining linear pencil. The certificate comes with an explicit complexity bound independent of the dimension of the coefficient Hilbert space. As a consequence, we solve the operator-valued noncommutative rational analog of Hilbert's 17th problem: every positive semidefinite operator-valued noncommutative rational function is a sum of hermitian squares, and even a single hermitian square when the coefficient Hilbert space is infinite-dimensional. In contrast, the corresponding commutative statement fails for infinite-dimensional operator coefficients.

papers.title: PF-Exec: Large-Scale UAV Relay Load Balancing with an Anchored Potential Direction Decider and a Per-Dimension Gain-Learning Executor
papers.abstract: Relay load balancing in large-scale UAV networks requires joint decisions on association, bandwidth, power and hovering position, while the dimension grows with the number of UAVs and each UAV sees only its local state. This paper splits the decision into two layers. An anchored potential direction decider emits a closed-form target at every instant and returns its direction only. A gain-learning executor maps a local observation into a positive gain per dimension, composes gain and target, and clips the action against the physical single-step bound; the two layers form PF-Exec. The unit gain is the default start, so the executor reduces to the pure potential policy before training. The load is first-order homogeneous in bandwidth, making the bandwidth target closed form, and the position target is the demand-weighted centroid of the served users. The system uses a two-hop access and millimetre-wave backhaul link with soft association, a 3GPP UMa-AV channel with two shadowing layers, an OU-type social-force crowd and a quadrotor physical layer. Evaluation spans all fleet sizes, two crowd scenarios, independent seeds, the published baselines in their own settings and a degraded-information line. In the highest-pressure burst setting the fixed-step comparison breaks down on part of the seeds, losing fairness and mean load at once, while PF-Exec holds fairness near one. Among the ten comparison methods only the greedy heuristic survives that setting; its load variance stays far higher. Under stale global state and position noise the fairness index stays high at both largest-scale scenarios. Flight energy is nearly identical between the learned and the fixed-step executor, and three constants are fixed once across all settings. The convergence properties of both layers, from the truncated gain iteration to the perturbed tracking bound, are proved in the companion analysis.

papers.title: A graph discretization of the Steklov and Neumann problems on domains in complete Riemannian manifolds
papers.abstract: We establish quantitative spectral convergence for graph discretizations of the Steklov and Neumann problems for bounded domains in complete Riemannian manifolds. Our construction uses weighted proximity graphs built from maximal $\epsilon$-separated sets, with a correction to the discrete energy accounting for the geometry near the boundary. We consider two discrete Steklov problems: one defined using an averaged boundary trace, and the other using restriction to boundary vertices. Both approximate the continuum Steklov spectrum, but under different conditions on the discretization parameters. The additional scale condition required for the restriction-based problem is also necessary for spectral convergence. As a byproduct, we obtain quantitative convergence of the Neumann spectrum. The estimates are uniform under suitable geometric bounds.

papers.title: Learning Recommendations under Imperfect Human Compliance with Record-Level Differential Privacy
papers.abstract: This paper investigates human-in-the-loop recommendation systems, where effectiveness relies on human compliance and privacy concerns restrict the use of historical response data. The pro posed framework models the implemented action as a random response to the recommendation and formulates the recommendation mechanism as a decision-dependent optimisation problem under an unknown compliance distribution. A batched Gaussian process upper confidence bound algorithm is then adapted to learn from locally perturbed historical actions, providing privacy for individual raw records. The analysis establishes record-level differential privacy and derives high-probability simple regret bounds when the compliance distribution is unknown. These bounds characterise how privacy noise, batch size, and behavioural information affect the guaranteed quality of the learned recommendation. In particular, a known upper bound on the non-compliance rate enables the rec ommendation space to be screened before any private data are queried. Simulations of a fixed-state car-following problem with synthetic historical driver responses demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm and verify the theoretical findings.

papers.title: Isolation of $k$-cliques in uniform hypergraphs
papers.abstract: A copy of a hypergraph $F$ is called an $F$-copy. For any integers $k$ and $r$ with $2 \leq r \leq k$, let $K_k^r$ denote the complete $r$-uniform hypergraph whose vertex set is $[k] = \{1, 2, \dots, k\}$ (that is, the edges of $K_k^r$ are the $r$-element subsets of $[k]$). Given an $r$-uniform $m$-edge hypergraph $H$, the $K_k^r$-isolation number of $H$, denoted by $\iota(H, K_k^r)$, is the size of a smallest subset $D$ of the vertex set of $H$ such that the closed neighbourhood $N[D]$ of $D$ intersects the vertex sets of the $K_k^r$-copies contained by $H$ (equivalently, $H-N[D]$ contains no $K_k^r$-copy). We prove that if $H$ is connected and not a $K_k^r$-copy, then $$\iota(H, K^r_k) \le \left \lfloor \frac{(r-1)m + 1}{(r-1)(\binom{k}{r}+1) + 1} \right \rfloor.$$ The bound is best possible. This is a solution to a problem of Li, Zhang and Ye. We also provide an alternative proof for $r < k$. Both proofs introduce new ideas for establishing bounds on isolation parameters.

papers.title: Convergence Properties of PF-Exec: Homogeneous Structure, Anchored Closed Form, and Gain Dynamics
papers.abstract: This paper establishes a layered mathematical char acterisation of PF-Exec, the algorithm of the companion system paper. Demand-proportional bandwidth allocation yields an exact first-order homogeneous decomposition, from which the equal-load bandwidth target and its feasibility bound follow in closed form. The logarithmic knee view preserves strict load order and shares its global optimum with the Jain fairness index, while the demand-weighted centroid minimises the position potential. The damped softmax association block possesses a fixed point on the product of simplices. The truncated one-dimensional gain iteration admits a complete characterisation, with geomet ric convergence below the critical gain, initial-value-dependent bounded oscillation at it, and a family of bounded two-state cycles above it. A global invariant error ball and an explicit tracking recursion complete the execution guarantee. A numerical audit confirms the structural identities on every measured state and quantifies the local amplification of the coupled association and resource dynamics. Together, the results explain how closed form recovery directions and bounded adaptive gains provide stable execution without requiring a global Euclidean contraction assumption.

papers.title: Identifying Latent Neural Dynamics with Recognition-Parametrised Gaussian Process Dynamical Systems
papers.abstract: Neural circuits are densely interconnected systems, and many neural computations are thought to be mediated by the dynamical evolution of activity within these recurrent networks, a hypothesis often referred to as "computation through dynamics". Under this view, understanding computation within real neural populations depends on building models of the dynamical rules governing the temporal evolution of recorded high-dimensional neural activity. Most commonly, such models depend on explicit generative parameterisations of (i) the (nonlinear) intrinsic dynamical flow field and stochasticity, (ii) the (nonlinear) mapping from dynamical state to neuronal activity, and (iii) the variability of individual neural responses given that dynamical state. Misspecification of any of these components can bias estimates of dynamics and latent trajectories. In this paper, we circumvent generation-related issues by introducing the Recognition-Parametrised Gaussian Process dynamics (RP-GPdyn) model. RP-GPdyn models the dynamical flow field using a nonparametric Gaussian Process-defined transition function and models the relationship of dynamics to neural activity implicitly using the Recognition-Parametrised Model (RPM) framework. We show that this generation-free approach uncovers meaningful, behaviourally relevant latent variables and dynamics from both synthetic and experimental datasets.

papers.title: Hidden Geometric Structure Beyond Conformal Flatness
papers.abstract: We uncover a hidden geometric structure in holographic correlators of M-theory, despite the absence of conformal flatness. We study two-point functions of $\frac{1}{2}$-BPS local operators in the presence of a $\frac{1}{2}$-BPS surface defect in six-dimensional $(2,0)$ theory, dual to an M2-brane in $\mathrm{AdS}_7\times$S$^4$. We find that the infinite tower of tree-level supergravity correlators can be generated from a single lowest-weight correlator. After a simple reorganization of the rational terms, the generating function takes the form of a weighted average over the internal S$^4$, acting through additive shifts of the spacetime cross ratios. This reveals a remarkably simple geometric organization underlying the holographic defect correlators.

papers.title: Quantum Fundamental Groups of Spaces with Finite-Sheeted Universal Covers
papers.abstract: Discrete quantum groups have attracted much interest, but there was a lack of natural examples until Voigt constructed quantum permutations of finite and infinite sets in arXiv:2208.01310. In this paper, we construct the quantum fundamental groups that contain the classical fundamental groups as subgroups. This is a new class of natural examples of discrete quantum groups arising from symmetries of covering spaces in topology. We characterize quantum fundamental groups for a wide class of examples, including $\mathbb{RP}^2$. We show that these quantum fundamental groups are genuinely quantum for spaces with finite fundamental groups that are either non-abelian or of non prime order.

papers.title: SURFACE: Preference Distribution Matching on Pareto Fronts via Scalarization Steering
papers.abstract: Constructing a finite Pareto representation requires allocating a limited number of solutions across the Pareto front (PF). A desired preference distribution specifies this allocation by assigning more solutions to some PF regions and fewer to others. Scalarization generates Pareto solutions by varying objective weights and solving single-objective problems. However, a distribution of scalarization weights generally does not translate into the same distribution of Pareto solutions along the PF, because the weight-to-solution map is nonlinear and unknown in advance.To account for this distortion, we introduce SURFACE (Scalarization Updates for Redistributing Finite Approximations with Chart Estimation}), which adaptively updates scalarization weights to match a desired PF distribution. SURFACE estimates how each region of the weight grid corresponds to an area of the PF from the current scalarized solutions, then redistributes the weights accordingly. The method supports parallel, warm-started, inexact optimization with standard single-objective solvers. Theoretically, we establish that, under the stated regularity conditions, SURFACE achieves linear convergence of the preference distribution mismatch to a finite-resolution error floor of $\mathcal{O}(N^{-2/(M-1)})$, where $N$ is the number of adaptive weights and $M$ is the number of objectives. Empirically, experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate improved target-mass balance and PF coverage compared with established baselines.

papers.title: On discrete harmonic functions with non-negativity on a large portion of $\mathbb{Z}^2$
papers.abstract: An improvement of Liouville's theorem for discrete harmonic functions on $\mathbb{Z}^2$ was obtained by Buhovsky, Logunov, Malinnikova, and Sodin. Namely, they proved that if a discrete harmonic function is bounded on a large portion of $\mathbb{Z}^2$, then the function is constant. In this paper, we study the corresponding problem if we replace the boundedness assumption with non-negativity. We establish this non-negativity result in some classes of discrete harmonic functions (polynomial growth and finite-translation-rank). Moreover, we prove that if a discrete harmonic function is non-negative on a large portion of $\mathbb{Z}^2$, then it has at most exponential growth.

papers.title: Collective Tree Exploration with Predictions
papers.abstract: We study collective tree exploration with subtree-size predictions. In this problem, a team of $k$ mobile agents needs to explore an unknown rooted tree as fast as possible, and whenever a new vertex $u$ is discovered, the team receives a prediction $\hat n_u$ of the number of nodes $n_u$ in the subtree rooted at $u$. We provide algorithmic guarantees under two error measures: the maximum error $E=\max_u|\widehat n_u-n_u|$ and the multiplicative distortion $\mu = (\max_u\widehat n_u/n_u)(\max_u n_u/\widehat n_u)$. For the maximum error, we present a deterministic algorithm that explores any tree with $n$ nodes and depth $D$ in $O(\text{OPT}+E)$ rounds, where $\text{OPT} = \Theta(n/k+D)$ is the offline benchmark, and we show that there is no deterministic algorithm that admits an $O(\text{OPT})+o(E)$ guarantee. For the multiplicative distortion, we present several algorithms that induce a competitive ratio in $\widetilde O(\min\{ \sqrt\mu\log k, \mu\log\log k+\mu^{1.5} \})$, where the $\widetilde O(\cdot)$ may hide logarithmic factors in $\mu$.

papers.title: Creating Steering Vectors via Input Optimisation
papers.abstract: Activation steering influences a language model's behaviour by adding a steering vector to its residual stream during generation, but it requires white-box access to modify the hidden states at every generation step. We introduce ActGCG, a modification of Greedy Coordinate Gradient which optimises a suffix to match the target activations obtained by adding a steering vector to the residual stream. We further introduce universal suffixes trained across many prompts at once, a model-translation step that rewrites the suffix into human-readable text midway through optimisation, and a soft-suffix variant to remove the discrete token space constraint. We study two behaviours: steering a model to answer in German, and anti-refusal steering for jailbreaking. For German, a discrete suffix reproduces the steering vector's behaviour almost perfectly and transfers well across prompts and models. For anti-refusal, the equivalence is weaker, succeeding under a phrase-avoidance metric but only partially under the stricter HarmBench classifier. Our results show that a steering vector's behaviour is reachable from the input, with no access to model internals at generation time, up to a loss that depends on the concept being steered.

papers.title: The ISM-CGM Transition of a Star-forming Dwarf Galaxy Resolved in Ionized Gas Emission
papers.abstract: The circumgalactic media (CGM) of dwarf galaxies are expected to be tightly coupled to their star formation, as low virial temperatures imply a CGM rich in cold accretion and shallow potential wells allow for more effective feedback. In this work, we use Keck/KCWI and KCRM to spatially resolve the ionized gas at the boundary between the interstellar medium (ISM) and CGM in dwarf galaxy UGC 6578 (M* = 10^7.8 Msun), out to ~0.1 Rvir. We discover a clear transition between the ISM and CGM at 0.033 Rvir, where the Halpha surface brightness profile changes from an exponential to a shallow power law, marking the first such detection at M*/Msun < 10^8. BPT diagnostics and ionization budget calculations indicate that the gas in the inner CGM is likely ionized by the galaxy's own star formation activity rather than shocks or the UV background. Spatially resolved emission maps also reveal a kinematically distinct, low-metallicity clump embedded in the inner CGM, and we discuss the possibility that this is a direct detection of ongoing gas accretion. This work serves as a pilot study for the Baryon Recycling in Dwarf Galaxies Emission Survey (BRIDGES), which will combine spatially resolved KCWI observations of the ISM-CGM interface in low-mass galaxies with wide-field observations of diffuse ionized gas out to the virial radius with the MOTHRA array.

papers.title: RAZeR: Representation Aware Zonotope Reduction
papers.abstract: Reachability analysis is a popular technique for verifying the safety of a dynamical system under uncertainty, where the uncertainty is often represented by zonotopes. As the size of the zonotope representation typically grows as the reachability analysis progresses, it must be repeatedly reduced at the cost of additional conservatism. While various methods exist to reduce the size of the representation, combined advantages are not fully leveraged as only a single reduction method is typically used throughout the analysis. In this work, we show how dynamically choosing which method to use can yield significantly tighter results, thereby easing verification. This is realized by introducing a heuristic, derived from model predictive control, that accounts for upcoming propagation of the current zonotope. We argue that order reduction is not merely a post-processing step after propagation but also a pre-processing step that shapes how the zonotope evolves under the system dynamics. We evaluate our approach, RAZeR, on nonlinear benchmarks taken from the ARCH-COMP, where we demonstrate that RAZeR produces tighter zonotopes at a negligible performance overhead.

papers.title: ERGo: Energy-Efficient Hybrid Graph Neural Network Training on Processing-In-Memory Architectures
papers.abstract: Processing-in-memory (PIM) has been proposed as an alternative computing paradigm for training Deep Neural Networks, including Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Despite these advancements, training GNN workloads on PIM devices necessitates off-chip memory access. This off-chip access is expensive in terms of performance and energy, thereby impacting the overall energy efficiency of the training process on PIM platforms. In this paper, we propose a novel hybrid training framework called ERGo that automatically switches from a full-parameter phase to a parameter-efficient phase during the training process with negligible loss in predictive accuracy. The parameter-efficient phase employs low-rank representations of GNN weights, effectively reducing the number of trainable parameters. This helps in reducing the off-chip access during the end-to-end training process on PIM architectures, leading to notable improvements in both performance and energy efficiency. ERGo outperforms the conventional full-parameter GNN training on a PIM-based platform by up to 3.15x in speedup and enhances energy efficiency by 10.5x. Furthermore, ERGo offers additional advantages when utilized on heterogeneous architectures incorporating non-volatile memory (NVM) and static random-access memory (SRAM). Training on the heterogeneous NVM-SRAM architecture typically utilizes NVM for the forward-pass and SRAM for the backward-pass. However, NVM cells suffer from low device endurance and repeated write operations due to weight updates can lead to poor lifetime. ERGo improves the lifetime of NVM devices by freezing the weights and preventing weight updates in the parameter-efficient phase. Experimental results demonstrate that ERGo improves the lifetime of heterogeneous NVM-SRAM architecture by up to 33x in comparison to full-parameter implementation.

papers.title: First-order characterizations of strong quasiconvexity with the exact modulus
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study first-order characterizations of strong quasiconvexity for functions defined on convex subsets of real normed spaces. For functions that are continuous along segments, an inequality involving the lower Dini derivative is a known necessary condition for strong quasiconvexity with a given modulus, whereas the established converse guarantees only half of that modulus. By means of a one-dimensional lemma, we prove that this inequality, and even its weaker version with the upper Dini derivative, ensures strong quasiconvexity with the same modulus, without requiring the domain to be open; this answers a question raised in the recent literature. The main result leads to a characterization with the same modulus in terms of the Clarke subdifferential for locally Lipschitz functions on Banach spaces, which answers another open question, and to a formula for the exact modulus of radial functions defined on Hilbert spaces. We also present some consequences in optimization, such as an optimality condition without Clarke regularity, an error bound with optimal constant and, for the projected subgradient method, the same convergence rate as in the strongly convex case, together with the exponential convergence of the associated flow. Finally, we show that the converse of a relation between proximal points and strong subdifferentials fails in general, but holds for a truncation of the function.

papers.title: Ozone groups and fixed rings of double Ore extensions
papers.abstract: We determine centers of two families of four-dimensional double Ore extensions without torsion assumptions, restricting to $f\ne0$ in $\mathcal O$. On the PI locus of $\mathcal K$, we classify the ozone groups and obtain normal commutative fixed rings of generic degree two over the center, including a nonmonogenic example. For an odd-torsion subfamily of $\mathcal O$, independent odd orders $n\geq1,m>1$ yield ozone group $C_n^2\times C_2^2$, PI degree $2nm$ and fixed-algebra PI degree $m$, with unchanged center. A PI specialization of $\mathcal G$ has trivial ozone group.

papers.title: Forcing global $\Pi^2_n$ uniformization with or without projective determinacy
papers.abstract: We construct a set-forcing extension of $L$ which has the same reals as $L$ and satisfies the $\Pi^2_n$-uniformization property for every $n\geq1$. Assuming $\omega$ Woodin cardinals and a measurable cardinal above them, we also obtain a forcing extension of $L(\mathbb R)^{M_\omega}$ which has the same reals and satisfies projective determinacy together with the $\Pi^2_n$-uniformization property for every $n\geq1$.

papers.title: CAT(0) Coxeter cell complexes, Bipodality and the Parallel Wall Property
papers.abstract: Coxeter cell complexes are a simultaneous generalization to cube complexes and the Davis complex of a Coxeter group. We show that 1-skeleta of CAT(0) Coxeter cell complexes isometrically embed into a CAT(0) cube complex. When the resulting cube complex is finite dimensional, we show that the condition of bipodality (satisfied by both CAT(0) cube complexes and Davis complexes of Coxeter groups) implies local finiteness of the cubulation. To this end, we show a Parallel Wall Theorem for bipodal CAT(0) Coxeter cell complexes satisfying a uniform bound on the size of a collection of pairwise intersecting walls. In particular, our methods give a new, purely geometric proof of the Parallel Wall Theorem for Coxeter groups.

papers.title: Do Mixture-of-Experts Routers Benefit from Ensembling?
papers.abstract: Ensembles of neural networks have repeatedly been shown to outperform single networks. Ensemble theory attributes this gain to the accuracy of the individual members and the diversity among them. Mixture-of-experts models already combine many experts, but a single router decides how the experts are weighted for each input. Motivated by ensemble theory, we apply ensembling to the routing step: an ensemble of routers, trained jointly with the experts, proposes the expert weights. We systematically evaluate this approach using underparameterized networks on two image-classification and two tabular-regression tasks. We analyse each experiment with a performance-diversity decomposition of the router ensemble, which, to our knowledge, has not previously been developed for routers. We report four findings. First, more routers lower the validation loss. Second, training routers to explicitly maximize expert diversity improves the mean performance on three of the four tasks. Third, explicitly maximizing router diversity has no effect on performance. Fourth, combining router weights with the arithmetic mean works better than combining them with the geometric mean. Routing benefits mildly from ensembling, but this benefit is offset by the computational cost of training additional routers.

papers.title: Resilient Transmission of Highly Structured Light via Active Convolved Illumination
papers.abstract: Wave propagation through lossy and noisy systems as well as spatiotemporally dynamic random media often limits the complex information that can be reliably transmitted or retrieved. Progress in adaptive optics, wavefront shaping, machine learning, and wave propagation theories has significantly advanced physical and computational correction techniques. However, many approaches remain constrained by restrictive operating conditions, limiting their ability to meet growing application-specific demands, such as higher spatial resolution in imaging and greater data capacity in communications, particularly in highly dynamic environments. Recently, active convolved illumination (ACI) was proposed as a novel framework for preserving the spatial structure of optical modes during propagation through strongly distorting environments, such as atmospheric turbulence. ACI aims to bypass the prohibitive complexity of global distortion tracking by combining spectrally localized characterization with compensation using a correlated auxiliary source. Here, we provide a comprehensive review of ACI, detailing the formulation of correlation-injecting and auxiliary sources and the role of segmented reciprocal-space characterization and distortion compensation. We explore extensions in free-space optical communication and potential high-precision phase measurement, and numerically evaluate interferometric strategies for experimental implementation. This work highlights ACI as a potentially versatile framework for distortion-resilient light transmission, with broad interdisciplinary utility ranging from atmospheric physics and remote sensing to telecommunications, target tracking, and biomedical diagnosis, offering flexible deployment either as a standalone paradigm or hybridized with existing optical systems.

papers.title: Improved Regret via Variance-Aware Policy Optimization in Adversarial MDPs
papers.abstract: We study episodic adversarial MDPs with unknown dynamics and full-information rewards and achieve regret with leading term $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^3SAK})$. Here $H$ is the horizon, $S$ the total number of states across decision layers, $A$ the number of actions, and $K$ the number of episodes. This improves the two incomparable prior leading terms by factors $\sqrt{S/H}$ and $\sqrt{H^3}$, leaving a factor $\sqrt H$ to the lower-bound scale. We give a reduction from unknown to known dynamics for \emph{downstream-dependent} algorithms, whose policy at step $h$ is computed only from information at steps $h+1$ and onward. This reduces the remaining leading-order gap to finding a downstream-dependent known-dynamics algorithm with $\widetilde O(H\sqrt K)$ regret, which would yield the tight $\widetilde O(H\sqrt{SAK})$ leading term for unknown dynamics. We instantiate the reduction with VOPO, a policy optimization (PO) algorithm. Its improved guarantees follow from a variance-aware analysis enabled by a novel bonus, which we call the Stability-Matching Bonus (SMB). VOPO achieves $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^3K})$ regret under known dynamics with full information; its $\sqrt H$ gap to the target $H\sqrt K$ rate is inherited by our unknown-dynamics guarantee. We also show that with known dynamics and trajectory bandit feedback, VOPO achieves $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^2SAK})$ regret. Both known-dynamics guarantees improve the corresponding state-of-the-art PO bounds by a factor $\sqrt H$. A matching lower bound establishes that the full-information rate is tight in one parameter regime.

papers.title: A thorough review on Deep Learning approaches to 2D-to-3D Registration in Medical Imaging
papers.abstract: 2D-to-3D image registration is a key component for several medical imaging purposes such as intraoperative guidance, enabling the alignment between preoperative 3D volumes and real-time 2D images. While conventional optimisation-based methods often struggle with non-convex objectives, sensitivity to initialisation, and high computational demands, deep learning (DL) has emerged as a promising alternative, offering improved alignment robustness and the potential for real-time performance. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of DL frameworks developed to address the challenges inherent in 2D-to-3D registration. We first outline how core concepts of DL are adapted to the registration problem. We then examine recent methodological advancements from multiple perspectives, including pipeline design, architectural innovations, and domain adaptation strategies. Particular attention is given to quantitative metrics, highlighting how performance is defined and measured across studies. Across the 41 included studies, we find that direct regression is the most common pipeline (23 studies, against 18 iterative ones), that hybrid CNN-attention architectures are gaining ground, and that research remains heavily concentrated on X-ray-to-CT registration. We conclude by identifying the absence of per-case uncertainty estimation and the strong neglect of temporal or sequential modelling as the two methodological gaps most consequential for clinical readiness, and discuss state-space models as a way to add temporal memory within intraoperative latency budgets. Further opportunities lie in more principled domain adaptation and in the integration of foundation models for representation learning.

papers.title: Geometric Bounds on Axion-Photon Couplings in Non-Supersymmetric Heterotic Compactifications
papers.abstract: We study the photon couplings of QCD axions and axion-like particles in non-supersymmetric heterotic string theory on Calabi-Yau threefolds with line bundles. After the St\"uckelberg mechanism and anomaly matching are taken into account, the QCD axion direction is determined by the QCD axion-coupling coefficients together with the axion kinetic matrix. We focus on the electromagnetic-to-color axion coupling ratio, $E/N$. When the physical electromagnetic and QCD axion-coupling vectors are proportional with the ratio fixed by the gauge levels, the QCD axion has $E/N=8/3$ for $k_3=k_2=1$ and $k_Y=5/3$, independently of the axion kinetic matrix. It is found that direct flux breaking of the visible $SO(16)_{\rm v}$ can produce independent QCD and electromagnetic axion-coupling vectors for the same level assignment. The Hermitian Yang-Mills equations and the heterotic Bianchi identity then restrict the departure from $8/3$. We derive analytic bounds for backgrounds with and without five-brane charge under assumptions about the axion kinetic terms and low-energy matching. An $SU(5)$-like model and a direct-flux Standard-Model-like model illustrate proportional and independent Green-Schwarz coupling vectors, respectively. For axions with no QCD coupling, we derive a geometric upper bound on their photon couplings and evaluate it in an explicit compactification.

papers.title: Use-case-driven ontology modeling with the NeOn methodology for ambient assisted living
papers.abstract: Research on smart homes and ambient assisted living (AAL) has grown steadily over the last decade, driven largely by the ageing of the population. A smart home has to coordinate heterogeneous smart objects in order to offer services tailored to its dwellers, and this requires a shared formal description of both the dwellers and the devices. We present the ontology developed as the semantic data layer of the Virtual Home Framework in the Italian Design For All project. Its requirements are derived from two use cases: a frail elderly woman who exercises at home on a cycle-ergometer, and a designer who configures a kitchen for users with different impairments. The requirements are collected in an Ontology Requirements Specification Document and the ontology is built with the NeOn methodology, reusing and reengineering existing ontologies where possible. The resulting modular ontology describes users through the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) and through their cardiorespiratory fitness; it also describes smart objects, their programs, the measurements they produce, and the comfort dimensions of the home. SWRL rules classify fitness levels, suggest exercise loads, assess indoor comfort, and identify the smart objects suited to a given impairment.

papers.title: Dimension bounds for higher Bruhat orders
papers.abstract: We study the Dushnik-Miller dimension of higher Bruhat orders. For the inclusion order $B_{\mathrm{inc}}(n,k)$, with $k$ fixed, we prove that the order of dimension growth is $n^k$, by exhibiting standard examples for the lower bound and explicit systems of coordinates for the upper bound. A recent Tur\'an-system construction of Gao, Kuang, Pikhurko and Wang gives an upper coefficient within a factor smaller than $4$ of the lower coefficient. For the genuine higher Bruhat order $B(n,k)$, we construct for every fixed $k\ge3$ a standard example of order $n^{2k+1}$. We leave it open whether a polynomial upper bound on this dimension exists.

papers.title: Poetry 'resurrection' from LLMs
papers.abstract: In an era where linguistic creativity is challenged by algorithmic authorship, we pose a provocative question: can artificial intelligence (AI) write an infinite poem? We set up two experiments to investigate the quantitative and qualitative output produced by AI utilizing couplets that evidence a poetic relationship between end words, the only variation in a strict anaphoric, litany structure. Our results show that while AI can generate interesting pairings, it still falls short of human-level creativity and understanding of poetic relationships. We offer commentary and a brief survey of the field of computational poetry experiments, tracing back authorial intention and distinctions of 'natural' and 'artificial' poetry, as well as justifying why couplet form is suited to testing AI's poetic output. Experiment 1 relies on manual prompting and co-creation to extend the original poem, which is developed into an animated webpage installation and interactive artwork. Experiment 2 reliably achieves automated output reaching the 1000 benchmark via an alternative method of using an LLM in combination with semantic similarity, of which Method 2 demonstrates a higher capacity for semantic and quantitative poetic output. These experiments highlight the limitations of current LLMs' generation capacity at the word level but also suggest that poetry will also respond and revive by incorporating AI workflows.

papers.title: Availability-Aware Historical Feedback Learning for Electric Arc Furnace Temperature and Chemical Composition Prediction
papers.abstract: Electric arc furnace (EAF) steelmaking plays an increasingly important role in recycled and lower-carbon steel production. However, variability in charged materials, energy input, and operating conditions makes accurate prediction of molten steel temperature and final chemical composition challenging. Intermittent or delayed measurements limit the information available for timely prediction. This study develops an availability-aware historical-feedback learning framework for predicting EAF endpoint temperature and the final concentrations of twelve chemical elements. Eight industrial data sources are integrated into three progressively enriched predictor representations comprising 19 static, 39 temporal, and 47 history-informed features. Historical outcomes are incorporated only when eligible under an assumed 60-minute measurement-release delay. Using 19,738 temperature heats and 3,341 chemistry heats, twelve tuned regression algorithms are evaluated through chronological forward validation. The proposed historical-feedback representation reduces root mean squared error (RMSE) in 147 of 156 matched algorithm-target comparisons. For temperature prediction, ExtraTrees achieves an RMSE of 12.290 degrees C, representing a 5.54 percent reduction compared with its temporal-only counterpart. Historical-feature ablation and feedback-delay sensitivity analyses demonstrate the importance of recent outcome information and its availability. In a separate retrospective later-period evaluation, lightweight adaptive residual correction reduces temperature RMSE from 12.502 to 12.275 degrees C without retraining the underlying model. Exploratory deep learning comparisons and target-specific feature-attribution analyses provide additional insights into predictive behavior. The results establish historical outcome availability and sequential feedback as important considerations for EAF endpoint prediction.

papers.title: Diffusion Tree Sampling for Inference Time Adaptation of Crystal Generative Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion-based generative models have become strong priors over plausible crystal structures, but turning that prior into promising candidates requires steering toward several conflicting properties at once. Fine-tuning is expensive and produces a new model for every new objective, while differentiable guidance is not applicable to many real-world tasks. We instead adapt these generative models at inference time using Diffusion Tree Sampling (DTS), a Monte Carlo tree search procedure over the denoising trajectory. We make two technical contributions on top of DTS that are particularly relevant for AI-for-science applications. First, we show how to use existing property-conditional generative models (e.g., models fine-tuned for classifier-free guidance) as guided proposals inside DTS, without distorting the target distribution. Second, we extend DTS to multi-objective sampling, so that a single search produces samples spanning an entire Pareto front. We instantiate both adaptations on de novo crystal generation: improving the stability of crystals generated by different models, using pretrained conditional models to generate crystals belonging to rare space groups or with high bulk modulus, and generating crystals along a Pareto front of high dielectric constant and high bandgap materials. Across these tasks, DTS-based inference-time adaptation successfully improves model outputs without modifying the models themselves.

papers.title: Tracing Knowledge and Reasoning in LLM
papers.abstract: Current evaluations of Large Language Models (LLMs) report performance at the dataset or task level, revealing what a model achieves but offering little insight into the internal processing associated with its performance. We propose a task-centric framework for characterising the model-internal processing elicited by a benchmark. It combines attention- and activation-based signals with representation-based measures to characterise benchmarks spanning a continuum from retrieval-dominant to reasoning-dominant and to surface failure modes that task-level scores conceal. We evaluate 16 LLMs across 24 diverse benchmarks and conduct targeted internal-state analyses on representative models and tasks, observing systematic differences in processing between knowledge-centric and reasoning-centric tasks. We shift evaluation from asking what score a model achieves toward characterising the processing patterns associated with that score, potentially supporting more targeted benchmark selection and more informed model choice. We open source our code at https://github.com/extraordinarylab/trace-kr.

papers.title: Unfinished-Bench: Measuring Rule Violations by Persistent Agents in Realistic Work Environments
papers.abstract: AI agents are increasingly equipped with persistence toward task completion to run delegated work autonomously for long periods, under many unstated constraints from internal documents and other people's authority. When completion requires violating a rule, the agent must decide alone, yet benchmarks of instruction-rule conflicts state the rule in the prompt or keep it hidden and do not evaluate persistence. We present Unfinished-Bench, a benchmark that gives models persistence in autonomous runs without a user, in realistic work environments with embedded rules. In each of its 97 scenarios across 7 organizations and 7 risk categories, the goal and the rule cannot both hold. We find that persistence raised violations of a rule in an internal document from 32.2% to 43.6%, five times the 8.5% for the same rule stated by the user. Of the document-rule violations, 98.3% occurred after the rule was displayed, and in 89% of a judged sample the agent first wrote down the rule. Violations of rules placed in the environment without user oversight can lead to serious incidents, so persistence-driven risks need to be evaluated. Benchmark documentation: https://francis21c.github.io/unfinished-bench/

papers.title: Classification with Large-Step Gradient Descent: Unifying Self-Stabilization and Convergence Rates
papers.abstract: Neural networks are often trained with gradient descent (GD) using step sizes that exceed classical stability thresholds, a regime where standard convergence theory no longer applies. Despite exhibiting non-monotonic loss and oscillatory dynamics, this regime frequently leads to faster convergence and better generalization. Existing theoretical perspectives offer complementary but incomplete insights: one identifies a self-stabilization mechanism that drives GD toward flat regions but does not yield convergence rates; another derives rigorous rates for specific losses but does not explain the underlying stabilization mechanism; and a third unifies these views for overparameterized least squares, but relies on the existence of a minimizer manifold, which is absent in classification settings. In this work, we extend this unified geometric perspective to exponential-tail losses, including logistic and cross-entropy losses in separable linear classification, where the loss infimum is not attained at any finite parameter. We identify a curvature-defined reference subspace that replaces the role of the minimizer manifold, yielding a coupled dynamical system in which orthogonal oscillations are damped by parallel progress along directions of decreasing sharpness. Under regularity conditions, which we verify for logistic and multiclass cross-entropy losses on symmetric data models, we derive explicit bounds for the iterates, not just the loss, covering both the unstable and stable regimes, and revealing a three-phase damping structure in the latter. Our analysis further uncovers a transient implicit bias induced by large step sizes: although GD converges asymptotically to the max-margin direction, large steps can leave persistent orthogonal residuals and, in certain geometries, amplify them, affecting finite-time alignment with the max-margin direction.

papers.title: FOMOS: Feature-Oriented Meshing of SDFs
papers.abstract: We introduce FOMOS, a purely geometric method for feature-oriented meshing of signed distance functions (SDFs) that addresses various challenges of the existing state-of-the-art methods. Our algorithm improves mesh quality and runtime, enabling the SDF meshing in a matter of seconds. While existing techniques such as Marching Cubes and Neural Dual Contouring either produce dense, low-quality triangulations or sacrifice details for sparsity, often requiring carefully chosen user parameters, our single-parameter FOMOS leverages feature sized sampling to dynamically adjust mesh resolution based on local feature size (LFS), which we compute efficiently by sampling a medial scaffold. The LFS considers not only curvature but also shape thickness and captures large features through non-local structure, omitting many redundant small triangles from existing methods. Through extensive comparisons, we demonstrate the distinct strengths of FOMOS in execution time, reconstructed result accuracy, and triangle quality in the output mesh. We also introduce a lightweight variant of FOMOS targeting huge ($10k^3$) sparse inputs, which, to the best of our knowledge, no existing method can handle except Marching Cubes. To demonstrate the usefulness of our method, we show that FOMOS enables instant previews using a sub-sampled medial scaffold and can accelerate volumetric simulations by orders of magnitude.

papers.title: Polynomial integrals and Poisson structures of the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator
papers.abstract: We classify the autonomous polynomial integrals of the nondegenerate fourth-order Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator. For a rational frequency ratio $m:n$ in lowest terms, the two sector energies together with the real and imaginary parts of a single ladder product generate all polynomial integrals, subject to one defining relation. The smallest total degree of an integral not expressible through the sector energies is $m+n$, and this bound is attained. For an irrational ratio only polynomials in the sector energies are conserved. In normal-mode variables the commensurate case is the negative oscillator resonance, and the classification realizes its invariant theory in the original higher-derivative variables. Two compatible Poisson structures generate the same dynamics with an indefinite and a positive-definite Hamiltonian. They induce different brackets on the same physical generators. We show that diagonal rescalings of the generators identifying the two abstract Poisson algebras exist only when $m$ or $n$ is even, and that none of them preserves the physical domain of nonnegative sector energies. Finally, we express the generators in terms of the original coordinate and its first three derivatives. The classical multiplier identity gives their variational characteristics in closed form and shows that the additional resonant integrals cannot arise from point variational symmetries.

papers.title: Physical-Risk-Aware Decentralized Agents for Constrained Vehicle Communications
papers.abstract: Decentralized V2X resource control is challenging because each vehicle has only local observations, while reliability depends on network-wide interactions. We develop a physical-risk-aware spatio-temporal graph attention (PA-STGAT) framework for agentic V2X control. Each vehicle perceives its local interaction graph, retains short-term temporal context, and independently selects its PC5 resource and power. Network outcomes are used during centralized training to refine the shared policy. Transmitter-specific credits map reliability failures to individual vehicles. A dual-priced graph term further converts network violations into coordination signals for discrete resource selection, with higher priority on short time-to-collision links. Experiments show higher raw-policy reliability than the tested graph-based baselines. Under filtered execution, PA-STGAT meets the nominal empirical communication requirements across all five seeds, with tradeoffs among utility, delivery reliability, resource occupancy, and filter-induced repair. Compared with GNN+MATD3, it requires fewer resource repairs but achieves lower utility and mean delivery reliability. Mechanism ablations show that removing dual-priced graph coordination causes resource-selection collapse. Density and mobility tests characterize the operating limits of empirical constraint satisfaction.

papers.title: TSGP-2: On the Non-Linearity of Symbolic Regression Problems and How to Exploit It with Model-based Semantic Genetic Programming
papers.abstract: Model-based variation operators such as the one used in Transformer Semantic Genetic Programming (TSGP) are affected by possible biases of their training data. TSGP is trained, in particular, on programs generated by Genetic Programming (GP) runs on linear target functions, which leads to a bias toward linear offspring. This bias can hinder search performance on problems that require non-linear solutions. This work has two goals: first, it investigates the linearity of standard test problems such as the Feynman and real-world benchmark problems. While most of the structure of real-world problems can be well approximated by linear structures, the Feynman problems exhibit varying levels of non-linear structure. Thus, a proper variation operator of a search method should be able to create both types of programs, linear as well as non-linear ones. Motivated by this observation, we propose TSGP-2, which follows the functionality of TSGP but uses as training data programs from GP runs on both linear and non-linear target functions. As a result, the training data includes a lower share of programs that behave linearly (the share drops from 83% to 37%). With a higher share of non-linear structures, TSGP-2 outperforms TSGP on problems with non-linear structure, while performing similarly on linear problems. In addition, TSGP-2 is less biased toward linear offspring and is able to propose a higher number of meaningful non-linear offspring earlier during search, which coincides with better solutions. The findings underscore the importance of training data for a learned variation operator and emphasize that the biases of search operators should be aligned with the problems they are applied to.

papers.title: Efficient quantum-circuit simulation of classical control of computational order
papers.abstract: We show that quantum circuits with classical control of computational order admit an efficient simulation by fixed-order quantum circuits: any such transformation acting on $N$ independent quantum channels can be deterministically, exactly, and universally simulated using at most $N^2$ queries. We generalize these constructions to extended, bipartite quantum channels and quantum instruments, and demonstrate that they can be implemented catalytically, without consuming the additional $N^2-N$ queries required for the simulation. In the case of quantum circuits with quantum control of computational order, we prove a similar simulation result, but restricted to unitary input channels (hence non-universal). These results show the limitations of the computational power of these classes of transformations in the studied scenarios.

papers.title: Insights into low-ionization structures in planetary nebulae: near-IR longslit spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Context. Low-ionization structures (LISs) are small, dense clumps within planetary nebulae (PNe) that stand out in low-ionization emission lines, but the physical processes responsible for their excitation and the nature of H2 remain poorly understood. Aims. We aim to characterize the excitation conditions and mass content of LISs in two PNe through near-IR longslit spectroscopy of these structures, combining H2, Brg, and [Fe II] diagnostics. Methods. We obtained H and K band spectra with GNIRS at Gemini North for LISs in NGC 6818 and NGC 7354 --objects with confirmed H2 emission in their LISs. We applied H2 excitation diagrams, vibrational and rotational temperature diagnostics, classical near-IR diagnostic diagrams, and spatial profile analysis to constrain the physical conditions of the molecular and atomic gas phases. Results. H2, Brg, and [Fe II] emission are detected in all structures studied. The H2 level populations are consistent with predominantly thermal, near-LTE excitation, with excitation temperatures in the range ~1860-2450 K. The [Fe II]/Brg ratios are well below the values expected for shock or X-ray dominated regions, favoring photoionization as the dominant excitation mechanism of the atomic gas. A clear spatial stratification is observed in both objects, with Brg peaking closer to the central star and H2 1-0S(1) and [Fe II] co-spatial at larger distances. The warm molecular masses derived from H2 emission lines are consistent with those estimated independently from H2 column densities. Conclusions. The diagnostics presented here support a photoevaporation scenario in which LISs are dense clumps being progressively ionized from outside by the radiation of central stars, while their H2 cores remain self-shielded. A slow internal shock may release Fe into the gas phase. These results extend the molecular mass trend established previously to a larger sample.

papers.title: QuantumInputOutput.jl: A Julia framework for input-output theory with quantum pulses and the SLH formalism
papers.abstract: The interaction of traveling photonic pulses with quantum systems is a fundamental process for many quantum technologies such as quantum communication, control, and measurement protocols. The so-called SLH formalism, named for the triple of operators that parametrize the dynamics, in combination with virtual emission and absorption cavities provides a general toolbox to describe such processes. However, modeling open quantum systems driven by propagating quantum pulses becomes cumbersome once several components, channels, and temporal modes are involved. Here we present QuantumInputOutput.jl, an open-source framework that automates this derivation process: first, symbolic expressions for the Hamiltonian and Lindblad operators are derived using predefined SLH rules and symbolic quantum algebra. Next, the obtained operators are converted to (time-dependent) numerical matrices or are used to obtain higher-order mean-field equations. The numerical expressions are presented in a form immediately suitable for solving the time evolution of the master equation and analyzing the output modes via correlation functions. Besides its usefulness for numerical simulations, the framework also provides a convenient tool to derive symbolic expressions for one-dimensional quantum systems such as multilevel emitters in cavities or waveguides.
